pool.q: At 18 months of age, a child develops a comitant esotropia that measures 20 prism-diopters (Δ) in primary position at near and distance. The child is not hyperopic and shows no lateral incomitance. What is her most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Basic acquired esotropia develops in children after 6 months of age, and the amount of hyperopia is not significant. It may be precipitated by disruption of binocular fusion (such as due to hyphema, preseptal cellulitis, ptosis, or patching for amblyopia).
Patients with accommodative esotropia typically have hyperopia, with onset from 6 months to 7 years. Infants with esotropia, by definition, have onset prior to 6 months of age. Cranial nerve VI palsy would cause an incomitant esotropia.

pool.q: What is the principal reason that patients with oculocutaneous and ocular albinism have decreased vision?
pool.rationale:
Albinism refers to a group of various conditions involving the melanin system of either the skin and eye (oculocutaneous albinism, OCA) or the eye alone (ocular albinism, OA). All types of albinism have foveal hypoplasia or aplasia, iris transillumination from decreased pigmentation, and a characteristic deficit of pigment in the retina, especially peripheral to the posterior pole (figure). The figure shows: A. Transillumination of iris in albinism, right eye. B. Fundus in albinism, right eye, demonstrating complete lack of pigment and macular agenesis. C. Child with oculocutaneous albinism type 2 (OCA2). Note white hair, eyebrows, and lashes, and light-colored irides and freckles.
Decreased vision is due to foveal hypoplasia resulting in nystagmus. If a child has significant foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus will begin at 2–3 months of life. The severity of the visual defect tends to be proportional to the degree of nystagmus and foveal hypoplasia. Iris transillumination is a key diagnostic feature but is not visually significant.
Optic nerve hypoplasia (ONH), which appears clinically as a pale or gray and smaller-than-normal optic nerve, can result in visual field defects and a range of visual acuities (normal to no light perception). Children with bilateral ONH can have sensory nystagmus, and those with unilateral ONH may have sensory strabismus. ONH is not associated with albinism, but is associated with midline central nervous system abnormalities such as septo-optic dysplasia (de Morsier syndrome), which is ONH with the absence of the septum pellucidum and agenesis of the corpus callosum.

pool.q: A 6-year-old girl presents for her annual eye examination and glasses update. Retinoscopy demonstrates a spherical equivalent of -12.00 in both eyes. She and her mother both had cleft palates at birth, and her mother reports a history of retinal detachments in both eyes. What underlying genetic condition most likely is present?
pool.rationale:
The abnormalities described are suggestive of Stickler syndrome. Ophthalmic findings of Stickler syndrome include high myopia, optically empty vitreous, congenital glaucoma, cataracts, and retinal detachment. Associated systemic findings include flat midface, progressive hearing loss, Pierre Robin sequence (a series of anomalies caused by abnormal descent of the tongue, including cleft palate, glossoptosis, micrognathia, and respiratory problems), mitral valve prolapse, and progressive arthropathy. The most common type of Stickler syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a mutation in COL2A1, the gene that encodes for type II procollagen.
A mutation in OPA1 is the most common cause of dominant optic atrophy, which is characterized clinically by a gradually progressive loss of visual acuity. A mutation in the mitochondrial genome at the 11778 position is the most common cause of Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, which usually presents with acute or subacute, bilateral, sequential vision loss with central or cecocentral scotomas. A mutation in WFS1 may cause Wolfram syndrome (aka DIDMOAD: diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, optic atrophy, deafness).

pool.q: A 12-month-old boy presents with a slowly growing mass on the lateral orbital rim. On examination, it is a painless, mobile mass. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows a well-circumscribed mass fixed to the periosteum. What treatment is recommended?
pool.rationale: The question describes the classic presentation of an orbital dermoid cyst that is painless and most commonly located at the superotemporal orbital rim. These cysts can extend into the bony suture line. To prevent rupture of the cyst, which causes an acute inflammatory reaction, surgical excision is recommended. Radiation is not indicated. The lesion is not infectious, so antibiotics would not be effective. Percutaneous drainage would likely cause an inflammatory reaction, and without removal of the cyst lining, the lesion would recur.

pool.q: What is the most common cause of pseudopapilledema in children?
pool.rationale:
Pseudopapilledema can usually be differentiated from true papilledema by the absence of disc hyperemia, retinal hemorrhages, or exudates and by the lack of any systemic findings that are associated with increased intracranial pressure. The most common cause of pseudopapilledema in children is optic disc drusen (figure). Pseudopapilledema from disc drusen is associated with anomalous branching of the large retinal vessels. The drusen can appear within the first or second decade of life, as demonstrated in the second figure. Although some patients with drusen can be identified by funduscopic evaluation, occasionally it is difficult to tell for certain that drusen are responsible for the swollen disc appearance. B-scan ultrasonography can be helpful in this situation as shown. Computed tomography can also detect these drusen. Uveitis also causes disc edema, but not papilledema, as there is uncommonly elevation of the intracranial pressure. The presence of an intracranial mass or idiopathic intracranial hypertension results in papilledema, not pseudopapilledema.

pool.q: A 4-year-old patient has new esotropia of a similar angle at distance and near. His refractive error is +4.00 D. When he wears glasses with the full correction, his vision is good in both eyes and his eyes are straight. What type of esotropia is this?
pool.rationale:
Refractive accommodative esotropia occurs in the setting of uncorrected hyperopia with accommodative convergence with insufficient fusional divergence, leading to an esotropia. The angle is approximately the same at distance and near fixation and is generally between 20 and 30 prism diopters. The average amount of hyperopia in refractive accommodative esotropia is +4.00 D.
In high AC/A ratio accommodative esotropia, patients have an excessive convergence response for the amount of accommodation required to focus. The deviation is only present at near or is much larger at near. In divergence insufficiency, the deviation is greater at distance than at near. A sensory esotropia would apply if the vision in one eye were poor.

pool.q: A patient with a near esodeviation greater than 10 prism diopters more than the distance deviation is considered to have what type of strabismus?

options.a: high accommodative convergence to accommodation ratio (AC/A) esotropia
options.c: high accommodative convergence to accommodation ratio (AC/A) exotropia

pool.rationale: A patient with an esodeviation and a high AC/A ratio has more esotropia at near than at distance. A patient with divergence insufficiency would have more esodeviation in the distance than at near. Convergence insufficiency would also have less esotropia at near.

pool.q: When does gonococcal conjunctivitis typically manifest in neonates?
pool.rationale:
Neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis usually presents as bilateral conjunctival injection and discharge 3 to 4 days after birth. Initially, the discharge can be serosanguineous with copious purulent exudates developing later. Corneal ulceration and possibly corneal perforation can occur if the infection is not treated. Treatment requires systemic ceftriaxone with topical saline irrigation.
Typically, chemical conjunctivitis is seen within 24 hours of birth. Chlamydia typically appears 1 week after birth. Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is typically seen 2 weeks after birth.

pool.q: What is the most common type of leukemia in children?
pool.rationale: Acute leukemias tend to have the most severe manifestations, with a rapid onset and course. Leukemia in childhood is acute in 95% of cases and is more commonly lymphocytic than myelocytic. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most common malignant disease of childhood. It is responsible for 30% of all cancer cases. In the US, there are 4000 new cases per year. The most common ocular manifestation of leukemia is leukemic retinopathy; however, all ocular structures can be affected. Ocular involvement is highly correlated with central nervous system (CNS) involvement.

pool.q: What optic nerve anomaly is most likely to be associated with a basal encephalocele?
pool.rationale:
Morning glory disc anomaly (top [1st] photo) typically appears as a funnel-shaped excavation of the posterior fundus that incorporates an enlarged optic disc with elevated surrounding retinal pigment epithelium and an increased number of blood vessels looping at the edges of the disc. It is sometimes associated with a basal encephalocele, PHACE (posterior fossa malformations, hemangiomas, arterial lesions, cardiac and eye anomalies) syndrome, and moyamoya disease.
Optic nerve hypoplasia (2nd photo) is associated with pituitary abnormalities and septo-optic dysplasia, not basal encephalocele. An optic nerve pit (3rd photo) represents herniation of dysplastic retina into a collagen-lined pocket extending posteriorly, often into the subarachnoid space, through a defect in the lamina cribrosa. Nevertheless, an optic nerve pit is not associated with encephalocele. Optic nerve coloboma (4th photo) is associated with CHARGE (coloboma, heart defects, choanal atresia, mental retardation, genitourinary abnormalities, and ear abnormalities) syndrome, but not encephalocele.

pool.q: What is the natural course of an eyelid hemangioma in a newborn?

options.a: regression for several months, followed by recurrence
options.c: growth for several months, followed by regression

pool.rationale: Hemangiomas (previously termed capillary or strawberry hemangiomas) are congenital lesions that become evident after the first few weeks of life. Treatment is indicated if the lesion involves the visual axis or causes some other amblyopic circumstance, such as significant astigmatism. The natural course of a capillary hemangioma is to increase in size until approximately 1 year of age, followed by involution over the next 4-5 years. It does not typically recur or regress immediately after birth.

pool.q: A child is diagnosed with orbital rhabdomyosarcoma. What is the most likely finding on examination?
pool.rationale: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common primary pediatric malignancy of the orbit, and is thought to originate from undifferentiated mesenchymal cells. The patient usually presents with rapidly progressing painless proptosis, globe displacement, and eyelid/conjunctival swelling. Proptosis is the most common feature, present in 80%-100% of cases. A palpable mass and pain are less common features, present in 25% and 10% of cases, respectively.

pool.q: What is the best test of binocular alignment to identify the presence of a tropia?
pool.rationale: Cover-uncover testing is the most important test to reveal a tropia. Alternate cover testing will measure both a tropia and a phoria. Worth 4-dot testing best measures suppression. The Lancaster red-green test is used for incomitant strabismus. Double Maddox rod testing precludes fusion and therefore does not differentiate between heterophorias and heterotropias.

pool.q: What is the essential feature of monofixation syndrome?

options.a: presence of peripheral fusion with the absence of bifoveal fusion, due to a central scotoma

pool.rationale: Monofixation syndrome is a sensory state in strabismus where there is the presence of peripheral fusion with the absence of bifoveal fusion, due to a macular scotoma. Thus amblyopia may be present in the deviated eye, along with a reduction of stereopsis. Because of peripheral fusion and anomalous retinal correspondence, the Worth 4-dot test demonstrates suppression at distance, but fusion at near.

pool.q: After attempted but unsuccessful treatment of his convergence insufficiency with orthoptic exercises, a 35-year-old man is unwilling to try adding prism to his glasses. What surgical procedure is most likely to improve his function?

options.b: posterior fixation of lateral rectus muscles

pool.rationale: Surgical treatment of convergence insufficiency is intended to improve ocular alignment primarily at near with reduction of the patient's exodeviation. This can be accomplished by lateral rectus recession or medial rectus resection, with no strong data suggesting one procedure is better, but medial rectus resection is more commonly chosen. Anterior transposition of the inferior oblique muscle can be used to treat dissociated vertical deviation. Recession/resection of all 4 rectus muscles can be used to treat congenital nystagmus in some patients. Posterior fixation of the lateral rectus muscles can be used for improvement of strabismus in high myopes.

pool.q: A patient is found to have A-pattern exotropia with compensatory head posture. What is the most likely head posture?
pool.rationale: In an A-pattern exotropia, the misalignment is more exotropic in downgaze and less exotropic in upgaze. Therefore, the patient may adopt a chin-down position to decrease or eliminate the misalignment. A chin-up position would worsen the alignment. A-pattern strabismus does not typically have lateral incomitance, so left and right face turns will not improve or worsen the alignment.

pool.q: What is the most common cause of visual loss in infants with abusive head trauma (previously called shaken baby syndrome)?
pool.rationale:
Intracranial injury in shaken infants almost always includes subdural hematoma over the cerebral convexities or in the interhemispheric fissure. Cerebral parenchymal damage is evident on neuroimaging as edema, ischemia, or contusion, and in later stages as atrophy, which leads to cortical visual impairment.
The most common ocular manifestation is retinal hemorrhage involving the preretinal, deep retinal, or subretinal layers. Sometimes the retinal tissue becomes disrupted, leading to full-thickness perimacular folds in the neurosensory retina and traumatic retinoschisis. Full-thickness retinal breaks and detachments are rare. Cataract formation and hyphema may develop secondarily to direct trauma to the eye, but not primarily from the shaking itself.

pool.q: What laboratory test is most likely to determine the etiology of anterior uveitis in a child?
pool.rationale: The most common identifiable etiology of anterior uveitis in a child is juvenile idiopathic arthritis, which occurs in 15%–47% of cases. Antinuclear antibody positivity is typically present in these children; rheumatoid factor is typically negative. Although juvenile spondyloarthropathies are associated with anterior uveitis in children, they are less common; thus, HLA-B27 testing is less likely to be beneficial. Infectious etiologies of anterior uveitis in children are less common, and results of serologic testing are less likely to reveal the etiology in these patients.

pool.q: A 1-year-old patient is diagnosed with pseudoesotropia. Cycloplegic retinoscopy is +2.00 OU. What is the most appropriate management?

options.a: reexamination of ocular alignment in 6-12 months
options.b: spectacle correction of full cycloplegic retinoscopy

pool.rationale: The illusion of pseudoesotropia is commonly associated with prominent bilateral epicanthal folds. Because no real deviation exists, results of corneal light reflex testing and cover testing are normal. The appearance of pseudoesotropia changes with growth of the nasal bridge and does not require surgical correction. The amount of hypermetropia measured in this child is age-appropriate. However, due to the hypermetropia and pseudoesotropic appearance, re-evaluation should be done to rule out the development of an accommodative esotropia in the future.

pool.q: What long-term refractive change is expected in the surgical eye of a 1-year-old child after an intraocular lens (IOL) is implanted?
pool.rationale: Because the child's eye continues to elongate throughout the first decade of life, the selection of IOL power is complicated. Thus, if a child is made emmetropic at age 1 with an IOL and the eye continues to grow, the result would be an increasing amount of myopia. These factors need to be taken into consideration when choosing IOL power.

pool.q: Wilms tumor may develop in 30% to 50% of children with what congenital disorder?
pool.rationale:
Sporadic aniridia is associated with the WAGR complex (Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary malformations, and mental retardation).
Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome is usually autosomal dominant, and 50% of cases develop glaucoma. Ocular findings in Goldenhar syndrome can include Duane syndrome, microphthalmia, upper eyelid coloboma, iris abnormalities, and corneal hypoesthesia. Weill-Marchesani syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive or autosomal dominant disease. Its ocular manifestations include microspherophakic lenses, severe myopia, and ectopia lentis.

pool.q: An 18-month-old child demonstrates an asymmetric, high-frequency, small amplitude ("shimmering") nystagmus, associated with head nodding. Neuroimaging is normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
pool.rationale:
Spasmus nutans is an idiopathic, asymmetric, high-frequency, small amplitude ("shimmering") nystagmus, associated with head nodding. It manifests during the first 2 years of life. The natural history is for the nystagmus and head nodding to diminish by 3-4 years of age. Spasmus nutans is a benign disorder in most cases, and management includes observation. Notably, because spasmus nutans-like nystagmus has been seen in the setting of chiasmal tumors, neuroimaging should be considered in these cases.
A Kestenbaum procedure is a surgery for nystagmus involving a recession-resection on both eyes. Vigabatrin is used to treat difficult-to-control seizures in tuberous sclerosis, and carbamazepine is used to treat superior oblique myokymia.

pool.q: What surgery would most benefit an 18-month-old child with a V-pattern infantile esotropia and bilateral dissociated vertical deviations?

options.a: bilateral medial rectus recessions and bilateral inferior oblique recessions
options.b: unilateral medial rectus recession and unilateral lateral rectus resection
options.c: bilateral medial rectus recessions and bilateral superior rectus recessions
options.d: bilateral lateral rectus resections with half tendon width inferior displacement

pool.rationale:
Children with infantile esotropia commonly have a V-pattern strabismus due to inferior oblique overaction. Inferior oblique recessions will address a V pattern and dissociated vertical deviation (DVD). Superior rectus recessions are done for DVD without inferior oblique overaction. Anterior oblique transposition is done to enhance the effect of the inferior oblique recession in these cases.
Unilateral recess and resect will not address the pattern or the DVD. Bilateral lateral rectus resections would address the esotropia, but a V pattern would be addressed by supraplacement, and this would not address DVD or inferior oblique overaction.

pool.q: A 4-month-old girl is brought for evaluation because her "eyes cross." Her cycloplegic refraction is +1.00 sphere in each eye. She has 40 prism diopters of constant esotropia in all directions of gaze. Using a toy for fixation, the ophthalmologist notes bilateral abduction deficits that resolve with patching each eye. No nystagmus is noted. What is the most appropriate long-term management for this patient to prevent the development of amblyopia?

options.d: patching each eye, alternating each day

pool.rationale:
This patient has infantile esotropia. Pertinent clinical features of infantile esotropia include a deviation characteristically greater than 30 prism diopters, overelevation in adduction, dissociated vertical deviation (DVD), and low hyperopia (1.00-2.00 diopters). Equal visual acuity is common, and an apparent abduction deficit may result from cross-fixation. The infant’s ability to abduct can be elicited by the doll’s head maneuver, spinning the infant to stimulate the vestibulo-ocular reflex, or by observation with either eye patched. These patients usually have full abduction unless there is secondary medial rectus muscle restriction. Hyperopia or astigmatism greater than +2.50 diopters suggests a refractive strabismus. Deviation in primary position of less than 30 prism diopters is uncommon in infantile esotropia.
Deviations greater than 30 diopters are unlikely to resolve and will probably require surgical intervention; ocular alignment is rarely achieved without surgery in early-onset esotropia. The belief is that the eyes should be aligned by 2 years of age, preferably earlier, to optimize binocular cooperation. The Congenital Esotropia Observational Study showed that when patients present with constant esotropia of at least 40Δ after 10 weeks of age, the deviations are unlikely to resolve spontaneously. Smaller angles can be monitored, as they may improve spontaneously. Full cycloplegic refraction should be prescribed, but because there is minimal refractive error, this is unlikely to fully resolve the esotropia (ie, minimal accommodative component).

pool.q: What is the preferred laboratory testing for a child with a unilateral congenital cataract?

options.d: TORCH titers (toxoplasmosis, other agents, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex)

pool.rationale:
Unilateral cataracts are not usually associated with occult systemic or metabolic disease; laboratory tests are therefore not warranted. It is important to note that bilateral cataracts can have significant asymmetry, however, so deferring laboratory tests should be done with caution.
In cases of bilateral cataracts, multiple components of the history and physical examination, rather than a battery of tests (a "shotgun" approach), can be useful for directed laboratory investigations. Part of the evaluation of pediatric cataracts should focus on cataract morphology (eg, nuclear, lamellar, anterior polar, posterior lenticonus, etc.). Family history is useful in some cases (isolated inherited cataracts are usually autosomal dominant). Other features that could suggest a need for directed testing include external appearance (eg, many craniofacial syndromes are associated with cataracts, as are chromosomal abnormalities such as Down syndrome, trisomy 13, and trisomy 18), history of renal disease (eg, Alport syndrome or Lowe syndrome), or history of metabolic disorders (eg, diabetes mellitus, Fabry disease, Wilson disease, etc). TORCH titers can also be useful in certain circumstances.

pool.q: The 3-step test for cyclovertical muscle function is a useful diagnostic test for what class of vertical strabismus?
pool.rationale:
The 3-step test is used to identify which paralytic muscle is causing a cyclovertical strabismus. The 3-step test involves determining: (1) the hypertropic eye with distance fixation, (2) whether the misalignment is worse in left or right gaze, and (3) whether the misalignment is worse in left or right head tilt.
This test does not work with patients who have had previous strabismus surgery, have a restrictive disease (such as thyroid eye disease), or have Brown syndrome.

pool.q: For a patient with dissociated vertical deviation (DVD), what motility anomaly accompanies the upward movement?

options.c: downward movement of the fellow eye on cover testing

pool.rationale: Patients with dissociated strabismus can have accompanying extorsion and exodeviation (not esodeviation) of the elevating eye. Typically there is no hypodeviation of the fellow eye on cover testing, due to an apparent violation of Hering's law of motor correspondence. DVD is usually seen in infantile strabismus. In this form of strabismus, any associated nystagmus is of the latent variety, which has a horizontal vector.

pool.q: After laser surgery, a child with retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) demonstrates a 30 prism diopter (∆) right exotropia on Hirschberg testing. When the left eye is covered, the right eye does not move medially. What is the most likely reason for this finding?
pool.rationale: Angle kappa is the angle between the visual axis and the anatomical pupillary axis of the eye. The fovea is usually slightly temporal to the pupillary axis, making the corneal light reflection slightly nasal to the center of the cornea. This is termed positive angle kappa. A large positive angle kappa (eg, from temporal dragging of the macula in cicatricial retinopathy of prematurity [ROP]) can simulate exotropia.

pool.q: How is dissociated horizontal deviation (DHD) typically treated?
pool.rationale: Dissociated strabismus can contain vertical, horizontal, and torsional components. When the dissociated abduction movement is predominant, it is called dissociated horizontal deviation (DHD). Treatment of DHD usually consists of unilateral or bilateral lateral rectus recession in addition to any necessary oblique or vertical muscle surgery. Base-out prisms and orthoptic exercises can be used to treat convergence insufficiency. Refractive correction of myopia can help control intermittent exotropia; however, DHD is not a true exotropia.

pool.q: What is the defining clinical feature of monofixation syndrome?

options.a: evidence of peripheral sensory fusion without central fusion
options.b: evidence of peripheral sensory fusion without motor fusion
options.c: evidence of central fusion without peripheral sensory fusion

pool.rationale: Monofixation syndrome describes peripheral fusion with the absence of bimacular (or central) fusion. The patient usually has a small deviation, usually less than 8 prism diopters of esotropia, which results in a central scotoma. Motor fusion is a vergence movement that is intended to cause retinal images to fall on corresponding retinal areas. This movement is present in monofixators, but central fusion is lacking as a result of the presence of a central scotoma.

pool.q: A child with cognitive impairment, seizures, and hypomelanotic macules presents for routine eye care. What intraocular finding is most likely to be observed?
pool.rationale:
The classic triad of tuberous sclerosis (known as Vogt triad) includes cognitive impairment, seizures, and facial angiofibromas. Facial angiofibromas are not usually present in young children, but hypomelanotic macules called "ash-leaf spots" are. The most frequent and characteristic ocular manifestation of tuberous sclerosis is retinal phakoma, or astrocytic hamartoma. Phakomas are usually located near the posterior pole and involve the retina and/or optic nerve.
Capillary hemangioblastomas are associated with von Hippel-Lindau disease. Choroidal hemangiomas are the most significant retinal anomaly associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome. Incomplete peripheral retinal vascularization and subsequent proliferative retinal vasculopathy can occur in incontinentia pigmenti (Bloch-Sulzberger syndrome) and closely resembles that of retinopathy of prematurity.

pool.q: What eye movement abnormality can occur in healthy infants in the first months of life?
pool.rationale: In the first few months of life, episodes of intermittent strabismus are common. Constant strabismus is not normal, even at this early age. Vertical nystagmus and ocular flutter are also abnormal.

pool.q: What feature of morning glory disc anomaly differentiates it from optic disc coloboma?

options.c: increased number of blood vessels coming off the disc

pool.rationale:
Morning glory disc anomaly (MGDA) is the result of abnormal development of the distal optic stalk at its junction with the primitive optic vesicle. The anomaly is typically unilateral and is more common in girls. A morning glory disc anomaly appears clinically as a funnel-shaped excavation enveloping the optic disc. There is an increased number of blood vessels coming off the disc, and a white tuft of glial tissue may be observed in the center of the optic disc cup. Morning glory disc anomaly is typically unilateral. Morning glory disc anomaly is associated with basal encephalocele and midface anomalies. It is also associated with moyamoya disease. Moyamoya disease typically presents with constriction of the internal carotid arteries as they enter the skull base and join the circle of Willis. Blood vessel constriction often leads to recurrent strokes, and patients may be started on antiplatelet therapy. Therefore, all patients with morning glory disc anomaly should have a brain MRI/ MRA to rule out these 2 conditions.
Optic disc coloboma arises from an incomplete closure of the embryonic fissure. Colobomas vary in appearance from small excavations that resemble glaucoma to widespread excavation. The defect typically extends inferonasally and may extend to the uvea. It is usually bilateral but may be asymmetric in appearance. Complications include retinal detachment. Visual acuity can vary from 20/20 to very poor. Ocular coloboma may be associated with systemic findings and a number of syndromes, including CHARGE syndrome: Coloboma, Heart (tetralogy of Fallot), choanal Atresia, mental Retardation, Genitourinary abnormalities, and Ear abnormalities.

pool.q: What is the leading cause of vision loss in the world, as well as a leading cause of visual impairment?

It has been estimated that by 2020, approximately 80 million people worldwide will have glaucoma, with 11.2 million bilaterally blind as a result. A meta-analysis estimated that the global prevalence is about 3.5%.

pool.q: An ophthalmologist is asked by the neonatal department to evaluate a premature infant for a possible embryogenetic defect. If the child has bilateral anophthalmia, at what stage did embryogenesis fail?

options.c: The choroidal fissure did not close.
options.d: The optic vesicle did not grow out from the cerebral vesicle.

pool.rationale:
The first step in ocular embryogenesis is the formation of the optic vesicle, which evaginates from the forebrain toward surface ectoderm. If this step fails, anophthalmia (also termed anophthalmos) results. The remaining choices describe progressive developmental steps in ocular formation. Multiple clefting patterns may occur in the periocular region; Goldenhar and Treacher Collins syndromes are good examples of periocular clefting abnormalities.
The choroidal fissure emanates from the ventral aspect of the optic stalk. It is most easily described as an anterior extension of the optic cup. Failure of choroidal fissure closure manifests as an iris coloboma.

pool.q: How do ductions differ from versions?

options.b: ductions are convergent eye movements; versions are divergent
options.c: ductions are binocular movements; versions are monocular

pool.rationale:
Ductions are monocular rotations of the eye. Adduction is movement of the eye nasally; abduction is movement of the eye temporally. Supraduction is an upward rotation of the eye, while infraduction is a downward rotation of the eye.
Versions are binocular eye movements when the eyes move in the same direction.
Vergences are binocular eye movements when the eyes move in opposite directions. Convergence is movement of both eyes nasally to a given starting position, while divergence is movement of both eyes temporally to a given starting point.

pool.q: A 2-week-old infant with leukocoria is suspected of having persistent fetal vasculature (PFV).  Anatomically, what globe size strongly supports a diagnosis of PFV over retinoblastoma?

Clinically, a retrolental membrane of varying size and density is attached to the posterior lens surface. In contrast to retinoblastoma, which typically occurs in normal-sized eyes, these eyes are nearly always microphthalmic (small and disorganized globe) to some degree. Nanophthalmos refers to small eyes (axial length < 18 mm ) that have a high lens-to-anterior segment ratio but otherwise lack disorganization. Buphthalmos ("ox eye") refers to diffuse globe enlargement, usually in the setting of congenital glaucoma.

pool.q: What is the earliest sign of anterior segment ischemia following strabismus surgery?

Simultaneous rectus muscle surgery, especially on 3 or 4 muscles (but also 2 muscles in patients with poor circulation) can result in anterior segment ischemia. The earliest sign of this complication is cells and flare in the anterior chamber, with more severe cases causing corneal epithelial edema, Descemet membrane folds, and an irregular pupil. In the most extreme cases, anterior segment necrosis and phthisis bulbi can occur.

pool.q: What is the most common cause of visual impairment in children with abusive head trauma?

pool.q: Most commonly, orbital cellulitis is caused by the spread of the infection from where?

pool.q: A 16-year-old boy with a history of a congenital cranial nerve (CN) IV palsy is found to have marked overaction of the inferior oblique muscle, underaction of the superior oblique muscle, and excyclotorsion in the affected eye. Symptoms of nasolacrimal duct obstruction, such as epiphora and periocular crusting, are often present. The differential diagnosis includes hemangioma, dermoid cyst, and encephalocele. pool.rationale: Topical anesthetic is most appropriate for adjustment of sutures postoperatively in adults. General anesthesia is necessary in children. Retrobulbar and sub-Tenon infusion are not indicated, because they can affect ocular motility.

pool.q: What is the most likely type of strabismus expected to be seen in a child with fetal alcohol syndrome?
pool.rationale: Fetal alcohol syndrome is a craniofacial condition caused by in-utero exposure to ethanol due to heavy alcohol use by women during pregnancy. Fetal alcohol syndrome is characterized by prenatal and postnatal growth retardation, central nervous system abnormalities, and a wide spectrum of malformations, the most typical of these being craniofacial. Pertinent facial features include short palpebral fissures, telecanthus, strabismus (especially esotropia), and ptosis. Ocular involvement can also include optic nerve hypoplasia (unilateral or bilateral) and increased tortuosity of the retinal vasculature. Nerve and muscle palsies and hypertropia are not components of fetal alcohol syndrome.

pool.q: An individual was involved in a car accident and has had vertical diplopia for 6 months. He has a right hypertropia that increases on left gaze and on right head tilt. The deviation is largest in gaze up and to the left. Surgery has been recommended. What procedure would be the most appropriate?

options.a: resection of the left inferior rectus
options.b: intrasheath tenectomy of the right superior oblique
options.c: resection of the right inferior rectus
options.d: recession of the right inferior oblique

pool.rationale:
These findings are consistent with a diagnosis of a right superior oblique weakness. The right eye is higher and the left eye is lower. The deviation is greater in left gaze. The muscle to be operated should be one whose greatest vertical action is in the direction of the greatest vertical deviation, which would be left gaze. Recessing the right inferior oblique (RIO) would lessen the hypertropia and would be the treatment of choice.
Resection of the left inferior rectus would increase the hypotropia of the left eye and increase the deviation. Resection of the right inferior rectus would lessen the left hypotropia, but since the deviation is worse in gaze up and left, it would not be the ideal choice. Intrasheath tenectomy of the right superior oblique would further weaken the right superior oblique and thereby increase the vertical deviation.

pool.q: A patient is found to have A-pattern exotropia with a compensatory head posture. What head posture is the clinician most likely to observe?
pool.rationale: A and V patterns are variations of a primary position horizontal misalignment, so there is no reason for a compensatory head position unless it allows single binocular vision. For a patient with A-pattern exotropia, single binocular vision, if achievable, is attained only with the eyes directed upward, so a chin-down head position is most likely. Head tilting or viewing in lateral gaze does not achieve this result.

pool.q: What should be the first step in examining a young child?
pool.rationale: The examination of a young child should begin with observation as the practitioner enters the room. Visual behavior, anomalous head posture, and dysmorphic features can be observed prior to the formal examination.

pool.q: What pattern strabismus would be most successfully addressed with bilateral weakening of the inferior oblique muscles?
pool.rationale: Inferior oblique overaction commonly causes a V pattern. A patterns are most commonly caused by superior oblique overaction. X and Y patterns result from pseudo-overaction of the inferior oblique muscles, and weakening them would not collapse the pattern.

pool.q: What is appropriate testing for diagnosing homocystinuria?
pool.rationale: Homocystinuria is an autosomal recessive condition associated with lens dislocation, with associated central nervous system and skeletal defects. The diagnosis is confirmed by detecting disulfides in the urine. Sulfite oxidase deficiency or molybdenum cofactor deficiency can also result in ectopia lentis. This enzyme deficiency interferes with conversion of sulfite to sulfate, resulting in increased urine excretion of sulfite. Increased sulfites and molybdenum cofactor deficiency are characteristic of sulfite oxidase deficiency. Epimerase deficiency is seen in a type of galactosemia.

pool.q: What term describes a small and disorganized eye?
pool.rationale:
Congenital and developmental anomalies of the globe include:
  • Anophthalmia is absence of any ocular globe tissue. It is very rare; usually, when anophthalmia is clinically suspected, the child actually has severe microphthalmia.
  • Coloboma is the most common and least severe manifestation of the MAC spectrum. It is typically an inferonasal gap in the iris or retina.
  • Microphthalmia is a small, disorganized globe that can be associated with cystic outpouching of the posteroinferior sclera.
  • Nanophthalmos is a small eye, typically with an axial length of 18 mm or less and with associated high hyperopia.

pool.q: What is the most likely ocular finding in a neonate with congenital rubella syndrome (CRS)?
pool.rationale:
A unilateral or bilateral pigmentary retinopathy is the most common ocular manifestation of CRS (25%–50%), followed by cataract (15%) and glaucoma (10%). The pigmentary disturbance, often described as “salt-and-pepper” fundus, shows considerable variation, ranging from finely stippled, bone spicule–like, small, black, irregular masses to gross pigmentary irregularities with coarse, blotchy mottling. It can be stationary or progressive. Despite loss of the foveal light reflex and prominent pigmentary changes, neither vision nor electroretinogram results are typically affected. Congenital (nuclear) cataracts and microphthalmia are the most frequent causes of poor visual acuity and, rarely, choroidal neovascularization (CNV). Unless otherwise compromised by glaucoma, the optic nerve and the retinal vessels are typically normal in appearance.

pool.q: What rectus muscles form the spiral of Tillaux, inserting closest to the limbus to most posterior from the limbus?

options.b: medial rectus, inferior rectus, lateral rectus, superior rectus
options.c: inferior rectus, lateral rectus, superior rectus, medial rectus
options.d: lateral rectus, superior rectus, medial rectus, inferior rectus

pool.rationale: The rectus muscles insert in a spiral, forming the spiral of Tillaux. The medial rectus inserts closest to the limbus, followed by the inferior rectus, then the lateral rectus, then the superior rectus, which inserts furthest (most posterior) from the limbus.

pool.q: What percentage of neuroblastomas undergo spontaneous regression?
pool.rationale: Neuroblastoma is a common childhood cancer that originates in the sympathetic ganglion chain or adrenal gland. It is the most common cause of orbital metastasis in children. Neuroblastomas undergo spontaneous regression in approximately 10% of cases.

pool.q: A child with tilted optic discs and vision difficulties at night should be worked up for what possible hereditary condition?
pool.rationale: A tilted disc appears as a disc with the superior portion elevated and the inferior portion displaced posteriorly. In addition, the disc may be horizontally rotated. Situs inversus (vessels initially go nasally before turning temporally off the disc) may be observed. Visual field may show a bitemporal hemianopia that does not respect the vertical midline, unlike a chiasmal lesion. Patients often have myopic astigmatism. Tilted disc syndrome is associated with X-linked congenital stationary night blindness. Congenital stationary night blindness is a group of hereditary conditions (X-linked most common form) causing rod dysfunction. Patients often present in infancy with nystagmus and a normal appearing fundus. However, some patients with the X-linked form present with myopic tilt and temporal pallor. Visual acuity varies from normal to poor. In CSNB, the most common ERG pattern shows a "negative" dark-adapted ERG: large a-wave with reduced (negative) b-wave.

pool.q: A toddler's parents bring him in for evaluation. They report that he fell and hit the side of a table at home. He is crying and examination is limited in the clinic. Examination under anesthesia reveals a small hyphema and heterochromia. In addition, there are small, round, tan, cutaneous papules on his face. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a self-limited, nonneoplastic histiocytic proliferation, occurring in infants younger than 2 years and typically regressing spontaneously by age 5 years. As in this patient, skin is involved as small, round, orange or tan papules. Iris lesions are unilateral and may occur either as small, localized, fleshy yellow-brown masses or be diffusely infiltrative, manifesting as heterochromia. The most characteristic clinical finding in patients with juvenile xanthogranuloma is spontaneous bleeding with hyphema. These patients may develop secondary glaucoma and significant vision loss and must be treated appropriately to avoid complications.
Child abuse must always remain in the differential in children; however, this patient has examination findings consistent with juvenile xanthogranuloma. Neurofibromatosis patients exhibit neurofibromas and café au lait spots different from the papules of juvenile xanthogranuloma. Furthermore, Lisch nodules in neurofibromatosis are not associated with spontaneous hyphemas.

pool.q: A child is being treated for orbital cellulitis and presents with worsening clinical symptoms. Orbital imaging should be performed to evaluate for what diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Orbital cellulitis, an infection of the orbit, involves the tissues posterior to the orbital septum. In children, worsening clinical symptoms are often associated with a subperiosteal abscess that requires surgical drainage; worsening symptoms are an indication for orbital imaging.
Preseptal cellulitis and eyelid abscess occur anterior to the orbital septum are less worrisome than orbital cellulitis and generally do not require imaging. Acute maxillary sinusitis is not usually associated with orbital cellulitis; ethmoid sinusitis is more commonly associated with it.

pool.q: A pediatrician performs the red reflex exam (Brückner test) on a 3-month-old infant. What does this test assess?
pool.rationale: The Brückner test evaluates the clarity and symmetry of the red reflex, identifies significant or asymmetric refractive errors, and determines the position of the corneal light reflex, which provides an estimate of ocular misalignment.

pool.q: What type of childhood cataract is caused by thinning of the lens capsule?
pool.rationale:
Posterior lenticonus is caused by progressive thinning of the central part of the posterior capsule. This thinning may cause an oil droplet appearance in the red reflex. As the outpouching of the lens progresses, the surrounding cortical fibers gradually opacify. This process can take many years, but if the lens capsule develops a small tear, rapid, total opacification of the lens can occur.
PHPV may have a posterior plaque. Anterior polar and lamellar cataracts are not associated with thinning of the posterior capsule.

pool.q: In congenital nasolacrimal obstruction, what is the most common blockage location?
pool.rationale: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction typically occurs at the most distal portion of the lacrimal duct due to incomplete canalization near full-term gestation (40 weeks) of what was a solid structure in the fetus. This blockage occurs at the valve of Hasner. The canaliculi and puncta as well as the valve of Rosenmüller, which is in the region of the junction of the canaliculi, are more likely to have canalized normally.

pool.q: What medication is the most appropriate treatment for an infant with ophthalmia neonatorum presenting at 1 week of age?
pool.rationale: Chlamydia trachomatis is the most likely etiology of ophthalmia neonatorum in this case. Systemic rather than simply topical treatment for Chlamydia is indicated because there is a risk of pneumonitis and otitis media. Doxycycline covers chlamydia; however, tetracyclines are contraindicated in children under 8 years old, since they can cause permanent discoloration of teeth. Topical ofloxacin (fluoroquinolone) and topical azithromycin (macrolide) would not provide systemic treatment.

pool.q: Why is active force generation tested in the evaluation of strabismus?

options.a: to differentiate intermittent from constant strabismus
options.b: to differentiate congenital and acquired strabismus
options.c: to differentiate paretic and restrictive strabismus
options.d: to differentiate horizontal and vertical strabismus

pool.rationale: Active force generation testing is indicated when there is a need to assess a muscle's contraction strength. An example involving extraocular muscles would be when differentiating a paretic from a restrictive strabismus. This test may also be revealing when deciding whether to recess or resect a muscle in a reoperative or a transposition procedure. Active force generation testing is relatively contraindicated in individuals with prior syncope or vasovagal reactions. It may also be contraindicated in individuals with filtering or inadvertent blebs if the globe must be grasped in the region of the elevated conjunctiva. Complications of the procedure include subconjunctival hemorrhage, which is expected, and corneal abrasion. The force generated by the levator palpebrae superioris or orbicularis oculi muscles is not usually assessed, because this information does not affect clinical management. Active force generation is not useful in differentiating an intermittent from a constant strabismus.

pool.q: Overaction of what muscle can result in an A-pattern strabismus?
pool.rationale: Superior oblique overaction results in an A-pattern strabismus and is commonly associated with exotropia. V-pattern and elevation of the involved eye in adduction are signs of inferior oblique overaction. Overaction of the rectus muscles does not cause A- or V-pattern strabismus.

pool.q: What is the most likely benefit of strabismus surgery for congenital nystagmus with a null point?
pool.rationale: Indications for strabismus surgery include improving functional vision by decreasing diplopia, relieving asthenopia, improving ocular alignment and establishing or restoring stereopsis, expanding binocular visual fields, or shifting best vision to a more central location (and by extension, reducing head turn). In congenital nystagmus with a null point, the null point may not be in primary gaze, and patients will adopt a compensatory head turn. A Kestenbaum-Anderson procedure shifts the null point to primary position. While some forms of congenital nystagmus are associated with strabismus, many may present in isolation. Strabismus surgery for nystagmus is not considered cosmetic, and strabismus surgery for nystagmus would not restore stereopsis.

pool.q: When performing cataract surgery on children, why is the capsulorrhexis a technically challenging procedure?

options.b: The capsule is thinner in children.

options.d: The capsule is more elastic in children.

pool.q: A 5-month-old boy has nystagmus and poor visual attention. The anterior segment is normal, but the posterior pole shows bilateral double-ring signs. What finding may be expected on neuroimaging?

When bilateral, ONH is associated with midline central nervous system (CNS) defects, with an absent septum pellucidum and agenesis of the corpus callosum; sensory nystagmus is also commonly present. pool.q: For high accommodative convergence/accommodation (AC/A) esotropia, what is the most appropriate initial therapy?

Alternate occlusion theoretically reduces suppression, but has no role in treating high AC/A esotropia. Base-in prism would increase the deviation in a patient with high AC/A esotropia.

pool.q: A child presents for a second opinion for chronic follicular conjunctivitis recalcitrant to topical steroids and antibiotics. The ophthalmologist notes a 2-mm skin-colored, dome-shaped mass on the eyelid margin with a central small crater. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Molluscum contagiosum affects primarily children 1 to 10 years of age, but adults may be infected from exposure to lesions, especially through sexual activity or if immunodeficient. The virus spreads from close contact (children at play, wrestling, sexual contact) or from scratching the nodules or coming in contact with fomites directly or through towels, communal baths, or tattoo instruments. The lesions typically last 6 to 8 weeks. Any area of skin may be affected, usually torso or limbs but occasional eyelids. The lesions are single or multiple flesh-colored, opalescent, and domeshaped, measuring 1 to 5 mm in diameter. A central depressed crater develops with a waxy core. The eyelid margin location may be associated with unilateral, chronic follicular conjunctivitis.
Multiple molluscum lesions in an adult should prompt consideration of HIV/AIDS. In contrast to other pox viruses, necrosis at the site of the lesion usually does not occur. Molluscum "bodies" can be demonstrated by smearing a glass slide with the material expressed from the central crater and examination with Giemsa, Gram-Wright, or Papanicolaou stains. Minor trauma (expression of the core, curettage, cryotherapy) often leads to regression. Eyelid margin lesions (usually single) may be removed by excisional biopsy and submitted for standard histopathologic diagnosis. This is usually curative for molluscum-associated follicular conjunctivitis.
Molluscum contagiosum is caused by a DNA pox virus (molluscum contagiosum virus-MCV). The virus has 4 subtypes (MCV 1-4), with MCV-1 most prevalent, but with geographic variation. MCV infects all layers of the epithelium, multiplying in the cytoplasm of squamous cells, eventually creating a central crater filled with debris, which includes viable, contagious viral particles that are easily shed or abraded. Pathologic findings are marked thickening of the squamous layer of the epithelium, forming expanded, localized intraepidermal nodules. The squamous cells are filled with granular material (MCV particles), which replaces the cytoplasm and compresses the nucleus, forming molluscum inclusions. The central crater contains a plug of necrotic debris, molluscum bodies, and contagious viral particles. The figures show selected findings.

pool.q: What imaging tests should be obtained in a patient with a morning glory disc anomaly?

options.b: brain MRI and abdominal computed tomography (CT)
options.d: brain MRI and magnetic resonance angiography (MRA)

pool.rationale: Morning glory disc anomaly (MGDA) is the result of abnormal development of the distal optic stalk at its junction with the primitive optic vesicle. The anomaly is typically unilateral and is more common in girls. A morning glory disc anomaly appears clinically as a funnel-shaped excavation enveloping the optic disc. There is an increased number of blood vessels coming off the disc, and a white tuft of glial tissue may be observed in the center of the optic disc cup. Morning glory disc anomaly is typically unilateral and visual acuity can range from 20/20 to no light perception. Retinal detachment is a known complication. Morning glory disc anomaly is associated with basal encephalocele and midface anomalies. It is also associated with moyamoya disease. Moyamoya disease typically presents with constriction of the internal carotid arteries as they enter the skull base and join the circle of Willis. Blood vessel constriction often leads to recurrent strokes, and patients may be started on antiplatelet therapy. Therefore, all patients with morning glory disc anomaly should have both a brain MRI and brain MRA to rule out these 2 conditions.

pool.q: An 8-year-old patient presents with lethargy, bilateral vision loss, bilateral pain with eye movement, and swollen optic discs. pool.q: Corneal light reflex (reflection) tests should be used to evaluate binocular alignment for what patients?

options.b: patients with good vision in both eyes
options.c: patients with mild amblyopia in one eye

pool.rationale:
Corneal light reflex tests are useful in assessing ocular alignment in patients who are unable to cooperate sufficiently to allow cover testing or who have poor vision in one or both eyes, and consequently have poor fixation. The main tests of this type are the Hirschberg, modified Krimsky, Brückner, and major amblyoscope methods. Children with good vision in both eyes will usually tolerate cover methods and do not display avoidance. The corneal light reflex method is less sensitive or quantitatively precise than cover-uncover or cross-cover methods, so it is less helpful in less severe amblyopia or strabismus.
The Hirschberg method is based on the premise that 1 mm of decentration of the corneal light reflection corresponds to approximately 7°, or 15 prism diopters, of ocular deviation of the visual axis.
The Krimsky method uses reflections produced on both corneas by a penlight and is ideally used at near fixation. The original method involved placing prisms in front of the deviating eye. More common modifications today involve holding prisms before the fixating eye or split between the 2 eyes. By adjusting the prisms to center the corneal reflection in the deviated eye, it is possible to approximate and quantitate the near deviation.
In order to perform the Brückner test, the examiner uses a direct ophthalmoscope to obtain a red reflex simultaneously in both eyes. Note that this test detects but does not measure the deviation. The major amblyoscope method uses separate target illumination, which can be moved to center the corneal light reflection. The amount of deviation is then read directly from the scale of the amblyoscope.

There is an increased number of blood vessels coming off the disc, and a white tuft of glial tissue may be observed in the center of the optic disc cup. Moyamoya disease typically presents with constriction of the internal carotid arteries as they enter the skull base and join the circle of Willis. Blood vessel constriction often leads to recurrent strokes, and patients may be started on antiplatelet therapy. Therefore, all patients with morning glory disc anomaly should have both a brain MRI and a brain MRA to rule out these 2 conditions.
Peripheral retinal nonperfusion has been reported with morning glory disc anomaly but is not common. Disc drusen and combined hamartoma of the retina and retinal pigment epithelium are not associated with this condition.

pool.q: What is the mechanism of action of botulinum toxin?

options.a: It blocks acetylcholine receptors in the postsynaptic motor end plate.
options.b: It persistently depolarizes the postsynaptic motor end plate.
options.c: It increases cholinesterase activity in the neuromuscular junction.
options.d: It prevents the release of acetylcholine from presynaptic motoneurons.

Purified botulinum toxin type A is used for various ophthalmic applications for its effect at paralyzing muscles in a local area. pool.q: An ophthalmologist is in the operating room to repair a globe that is ruptured due to a piece of metal that struck the patient’s right eye. pool.q: What is the most common ocular finding associated with nonaccidental abusive head trauma?

Violent shaking of infants is associated with ocular, intracranial, and other injuries. The historical terminology “shaken baby syndrome,” is still in use but being replaced by the preferred “abusive head trauma,” or “inflicted childhood neurotrauma.” Most often, patients affected are less than 1 year old, and often less than 6 months old, because a crying, inconsolable infant is believed to trigger a frustrated or angry caregiver. There may be a history of mental status changes with a reported history of minor trauma. In the United States and Canada, any physician suspicious of child abuse is required to report the case to the appropriate governmental agency.

Hemorrhages can be present in all layers, may be unilateral or bilateral, and often resolve quickly. Other ocular findings associated with abusive head trauma include circumferential full-thickness perimacular folds of the neurosensory retina, retinoschisis cavities (often partially filled with blood), and vitreous hemorrhage. Retinal breaks and detachments are notably rare in this clinical scenario. Adnexal and anterior segment injuries are also typically absent. AHT is associated with high morbidity and mortality. A mortality rate of 29% among a large cohort of AHT patients has been reported.
Long-term cognitive and motor dysfunction, as well as visual impairment are potential complications. The most common cause of vision loss in AHT is cortical injury, followed by optic atrophy, although dense vitreous hemorrhage can also be amblyogenic.

pool.q: A 5-year-old patient has acute, progressive erythema and swelling of the right upper eyelid. The patient has normal globe movement without pain, and there is no afferent pupillary defect. pool.q: What would be the most likely finding in a 15-month-old patient diagnosed with congenital fibrosis syndrome?

A third nerve palsy may present with unilateral or bilateral ptosis and limitation of adduction, along with limitation of supra- and infraduction while abduction is intact. Leukemic infiltration of the orbit can occur, but it is uncommon.

pool.q: What is the effect of a posterior fixation suture in strabismus surgery?

options.b: weakening of the muscle in its field of action
options.c: strengthening of the muscle in its field of action
options.d: redirecting the path of the muscle

pool.rationale:
A posterior fixation suture involves the attachment of a rectus muscle with a nonabsorbable suture 11-18 mm posterior to the insertion site and is used to weaken the muscle in its field of action without significantly affecting alignment in primary position. This procedure is particularly useful for treatment of incomitant strabismus.
Transposition procedures involve redirection of the paths of the extraocular muscles. Advancement of the anterior half of the superior oblique tendon reduces excyclotorsion in patients with superior oblique palsy.

pool.q: A 7-year-old girl has an acute-onset esotropia with diplopia. The esotropia increases in left gaze and she has a left head turn. Her visual acuity is 20/20 in each eye and cycloplegic refraction is +1.00 OU. What is the next step in management?
pool.rationale:
A sixth nerve palsy in an older child often presents with diplopia, a compensatory head turn toward the side of the paralyzed lateral rectus muscle, and an esotropia that increases in gaze toward the size of the paralyzed lateral rectus muscle. Vision is usually equal in both eyes if the child presents soon after the onset of deviation.
Because sixth nerve palsy in older children is associated with intracranial lesions in one-third of cases, neuroimaging is recommended, even in the absence of other neurologic signs.
Correction of hyperopia with glasses is the treatment for refractive accommodative esotropia. Patients have an average of +4.00 D of hyperopia.

Eye muscle surgery may be used to treat an esotropia secondary to sixth nerve palsy if it does not resolve, but it would not be the initial management.
Orthoptic exercises are helpful in the treatment of exodeviation caused by convergence insufficiency.

pool.q: A child has craniosynostosis with hydrocephalus, normal intelligence, and normal hands and feet. What craniosynostosis syndrome is most likely?
pool.rationale: Common features of the craniosynostosis syndromes include fusion of multiple calvarial sutures and skull base sutures. Syndactyly (partial fusion of the digits) and brachydachtyly (short digits) are hallmarks of the craniosynostosis syndromes, with the exception of Crouzon syndrome. Crouzon syndrome is the most common craniosystosis syndrome. Hydrocephalus is common but intelligence is usually normal. The absence of anomalies of the hands and feet can aid in the diagnosis of Crouzon syndrome.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An 18-month-old child with congenital jerk-wave nystagmus has dampening of her nystagmus when she crosses her eyes. Examination reveals nystagmus with attempted abduction and a head turn with occlusion of either eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Nystagmus blockage syndrome occurs because nystagmus is dampened by convergence. Classic findings are increased jerk nystagmus on lateral gaze, esotropia, and "eating up prism" on attempted measurement of misalignment. In some situations, it may be difficult to distinguish nystagmus blockage with resultant esotropia from overlying esotropia and nystagmus. It may also be difficult to distinguish from coexisting strabismus with latent nystagmus.
Möbius syndrome is not typically associated with nystagmus. Möbius syndrome results in incomitant strabismus (may be orthotropic in primary position [40%], esotropic [50%], or exotropic [10%]) from a cranial nerve (CN) VI palsy and masklike facies from a CN VII on the ipsilateral side. It is sometimes associated with limb, chest, or tongue defects. Poland syndrome with absent pectoralis muscle is a variant of Möbius syndrome.
Cyclic esotropia is not typically associated with nystagmus either. It has onset in preschool years, is comitant and intermittent, and usually occurs every other day (48-hour cycle).
Convergence-retraction nystagmus is not a true nystagmus, but a disjunctive saccadic oscillation. It is part of the dorsal midbrain syndrome, with other findings of paralysis of upgaze, eyelid retraction, and pupillary light-near dissociation.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the average corneal horizontal diameter in a full-term newborn?
pool.rationale: The average corneal horizontal diameter in a newborn is 9.5 to 10.5 mm. This diameter increases to 12 mm on average in an adult. The keratometry readings decrease significantly in the first 6 months of life as the cornea flattens with increasing diameter.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 5-year-old girl has cyclic esotropia, with esotropia occurring every other day. What would be the expected findings when her fusion and binocular vision are tested?

options.a: absent fusion and binocular vision on strabismic days, and improved fusion and binocular vision on orthotropic days
options.b: excellent fusion and binocular vision on strabismic and orthotropic days
options.c: absent fusion and binocular vision on strabismic and nonstrabismic days
options.d: absent fusion and binocular vision on orthotropic days, and improved fusion and vision on strabismic days

pool.rationale: Cyclic esotropia is rare and typically occurs in preschool-aged children. The esotropia is comitant and intermittent, usually occurring every other day (48-hour cycle). Fusion and binocular vision are absent or poor on strabismic days and greatly improved on days in which the eyes are well-aligned. Surgical treatment of cyclic esotropia is usually effective.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In differentiating true papilledema from pseudopapilledema what is the most reliable sign?

options.a: presence of shiny refractile bodies on the disc surface in papilledema
options.b: hyperemia of the nerve with pseudopapilledema
options.c: obscuration of the vessels at the disc margin in papilledema
options.d: blurring of optic disc margins in papilledema

pool.rationale:
Pseudopapilledema refers to any elevated anomaly of the optic disc that resembles papilledema. Conditions that are frequently confused with papilledema in children include optic disc drusen, hyperopic discs, and prominent optic glial tissue. Pseudopapilledema can be differentiated from true papilledema by the absence of disc hyperemia and retinal hemorrhages or exudates. With papilledema, there is obscuration of the disc margin. In cases of optic nerve drusen, trifurcated rather than bifurcated vessels can be seen emerging from the disc.
Other features associated with drusen rather than papilledema include refractile bodies on the disc surface, absence of hyperemia, absence of surface hemorrhages, presence of spontaneous venous pulsations in most, and normal thickness of the peripapillary nerve fiber layer. Blurring of the disc margin and elevation of the disc can occur in both pseudopapilledema and true papilledema. Identification of disc drusen on examination or with imaging studies confirms the diagnosis of pseudopapilledema.

pool.q: A developmentally delayed 5-month-old child presents with a constant 30 prism-diopter (Δ) exotropia that is comitant in lateral gazes. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
pool.rationale:
This patient has infantile exotropia. Infantile exotropia presents with a large-angle constant exotropia prior to 6 months of age. There is an increased risk of neurologic impairment and craniofacial disorders in these patients. The treatment of constant infantile exotropia is early surgery. Surgery can lead to monofixation with gross binocular vision, but restoration of normal binocular function is rare.
Correction of myopia and use of base-in prisms can be used to treat intermittent exotropia, but they are not helpful for infantile exotropia. Observation would not be appropriate, since infantile exotropia will not resolve on its own.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: When examining an optic nerve, what clinical finding may support a suspicion for optic disc drusen rather than true papilledema?
pool.rationale:
Pseudopapilledema refers to an elevated appearance of the optic disc mimicking papilledema. Unlike papilledema, pseudopapilledema typically does not have retinal hemorrhages, disc hyperemia, or vessel obscuration. The most common cause of pseudopapilledema in children is disc drusen. Other causes include hyperopia and prominent glial tissue.
Disc drusen is often inherited and becomes apparent in the first couple decades of life. Disc drusen may appear as refractile gray-yellow bodies if near the surface of the nerve. However, often they are buried and not clinically visible. One useful clinical finding often seen with disc drusen is anomalous branching of the large retinal vessels over the disc. Rare complications of disc drusen include subretinal neovascular membrane or hemorrhage. B scan ultrasonography and computed tomography are useful imaging tools to identify disc drusen. Patients with pseudoxanthoma elasticum have a higher incidence of disc drusen.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What type of urinalysis is the most appropriate for establishing the diagnosis of neuroblastoma?
pool.rationale: Neuroblastoma is one of the more common childhood tumors that frequently have orbital manifestations. The primary tumor is typically in the adrenal glands or sympathetic ganglion chain. Urine catecholamines are positive in 90% to 95% of patients. Urine glucose levels, red blood cell counts, and white blood cell counts are not helpful in making the diagnosis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the name of the clinical test of binocular alignment that makes use of the corneal light reflex, prisms, and pupil/iris landmarks?
pool.rationale: The Krimsky test uses the light reflections on both corneas and involves placing a prism on the deviating eye until the light reflex is centered. The amount of prism required to center the light reflex is equivalent to the amount of deviation. The Hirschberg test estimates the angle of deviation based on the millimeters of light decentration in the deviating eye but does not use a prism. The Brückner test detects but does not measure strabismus. This involves a comparison of the red reflexes. The Bielschowsky test is used to isolate a paresis of a cyclovertical muscle. This test does not involve the light reflex.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Ophthalmia neonatorum caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae has its onset typically how long after birth?
pool.rationale: Ophthalmia neonatorum is a conjunctivitis that occurs in the first month of life and can be caused by numerous organisms, in addition to chemical agents. Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes the most serious form of the disease and typically has a delayed but abrupt onset. It usually presents in the first 3 to 4 days after birth.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: The International Classification for Retinopathy of Prematurity (ICROP) defines stage 1 disease as having what finding?
pool.rationale:
The correct staging of ROP is necessary to determine treatment and screening protocols, as well as standardize research. Stage 1 ROP is defined as the presence of a demarcation line between the vascularized and avascular retina. In this stage, the shunt vessels are essentially flat. A ridge, where the shunt vessels at the border between vascular and avascular retina are thickened and elevated, is the definition of stage 2. Extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation defines stage 3. A subtotal retinal detachment occurs in stage 4.

(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)
