pool.q: What is the prevalence of amblyopia in the North American population?
pool.rationale: Amblyopia is the most common cause of monocular vision impairment in North American children, affecting 2%-4% of the population. Risk factors include prematurity, developmental delays, and a family history of amblyopia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 5-year-old boy presents with an esotropia that occurs every third day. The ophthalmologist confirms this observation and has examined him on a day he is esotropic and on days that he is orthotropic. What is the best treatment for this child?

options.a: surgery for the maximum angle of esotropia
options.b: observation to see if this will resolve spontaneously
options.c: patch 1 eye for 2 hours on strabismic days

pool.rationale: This patient has cyclic esotropia. Surgery for the maximum angle of esotropia is indicated. Any accommodative component should be addressed, but +1.0 refractive error does not suggest an accommodative esotropia, and glasses are not likely to be of benefit. This is not likely to resolve spontaneously. Occlusion therapy may convert the cyclic deviation into a constant one. These patients are not typically amblyopic.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 6-year-old boy with visual acuity of 20/400 OD and 20/20 OS has a cycloplegic refraction of +3.00 sphere OD and +0.25 sphere OS. He is prescribed full-time glasses. At the 3-month follow-up visit, his visual acuity is 20/200 OD and 20/20 OS. What is the preferred treatment for this condition?
pool.rationale: Refractive amblyopia frequently occurs in the more hyperopic eye of anisometropic hyperopia. If the vision is worse than 20/100, the preferred initial therapy is patching. Atropine is typically used in moderate amblyopia with vision of 20/100 or better. Bifocal lenses treat high accommodative convergence/accommodation (AC/A) ratio esotropia, not amblyopia. Other neurologic findings are rare in refractive amblyopia, and neurologic consultation is not typically needed.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An 11-month-old girl presents for evaluation and is found to have epiblepharon. The child is playful and asymptomatic, and there is no evidence of corneal involvement. What would be the best initial management for her condition?

options.a: surgery to remove a strip of skin and orbicularis muscle from beneath the eyelid margin

pool.rationale: Although epiblepharon can produce an in-turning of the eyelashes, there is often minimal or no irritation of the cornea. If no significant fluorescein staining of the cornea is detected, only observation is required. The epiblepharon often resolves spontaneously with time and seldom requires surgical treatment.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the maximum distance from the muscle insertion that an instrument can be placed during strabismus surgery without causing iatrogenic injury to the nerves innervating the rectus muscles?
pool.rationale: The nerves to the rectus muscles and the superior oblique muscle enter the muscles approximately one-third of the distance from the origin to the insertion (or trochlea). An instrument thrust more than 26 mm posterior to a rectus muscle's insertion may cause injury to the nerve.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What type of exodeviation is most commonly seen in the general population?
pool.rationale: Intermittent exotropia is the most common exodeviation. Infantile exotropia and type 2 Duane retraction syndrome are uncommon entities. Pseudoexotropia is the result of certain facial features or a structural abnormality of the retina and is not a true strabismus disorder.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What are the clinical features of Brown syndrome?

options.a: deficient elevation in adduction, improved elevation in abduction, associated with an A pattern
options.b: deficient elevation in abduction, improved elevation in adduction, associated with an A pattern
options.c: deficient elevation in adduction, improved elevation in abduction, associated with a V pattern
options.d: deficient elevation in abduction, improved elevation in adduction, associated with a V pattern

pool.rationale:
Pertinent clinical features of Brown syndrome include deficient elevation in adduction that improves in abduction but often not completely. Adduction is associated with widening of the palpebral fissure and a downshoot of the involved eye (figure). Individuals may also have a hypotropia of the involved eye in the primary position. Attempts to elevate the eye straight upward usually cause divergence due to resistence from the tight superior obliques, causing lateral diversion of the globe. This results in a V pattern, which contrasts with the A pattern exhibited in inferior oblique muscle paralysis. Positive forced duction testing confirms the diagnosis. Brown syndrome may be congenital or acquired, constant or intermittent. Acquired cases may result from local trauma to the region of the trochlea, systemic inflammatory conditions, or sinusitis. Computed tomography scan should be considered in acquired cases. Management can be medical and/or surgical. Spontaneous resolution has also been reported.

(A figure accompanies this rationale on the section page.)
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the reason to neuro-image children with small-amplitude, high-frequency nystagmus?

options.a: to identify possible pineal gland tumor
options.d: to identify possible chiasmal or suprachiasmal tumors

pool.rationale: Spasmus nutans-like nystagmus (small-amplitude, high-frequency (shimmering), dysconjugate nystagmus) can occur in chiasmal or suprachiasmal tumors. Pineal gland tumors can cause convergence-retraction nystagmus as part of the dorsal midbrain syndrome. Paraneoplastic effects of neuroblastoma can cause opsoclonus. Arnold-Chiari malformations can cause vertical nystagmus.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What characterizes the slow phase seen in ocular motor recordings of patients with infantile nystagmus syndrome?
pool.rationale: Infantile nystagmus syndrome (congenital nystagmus) has a diagnostic ocular motor recording of an accelerating slow phase. Fusion maldevelopment nystagmus syndrome (latent or manifest latent nystagmus) ocular motor recordings show 2 types of slow phases: linear and decelerating.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 6-month-old patient with strabismus, fixating on an accommodative target at 14 inches, is examined with a penlight. The corneal light reflex in the right eye is displaced temporally relative to the center of the pupil, whereas the corneal light reflex in the left eye is in the center of the pupil. The patient has what type of strabismus?
pool.rationale: Corneal light reflex tests are useful in assessing ocular alignment in patients who cannot cooperate sufficiently to allow cover testing or who have poor fixation. Two main types of this test are the Hirschberg and modified Krimsky. The Hirschberg method is based on the premise that 1 mm of decentration of the corneal light reflection corresponds to approximately 7 degrees or 15 diopters of ocular deviation, using the iris as an anatomical landmark. The modified Krimsky method uses the alignment of the light reflex by neutralizing with prisms. In either case, an eye deviated inward (esotropic) will produce a light reflex that is displaced temporally from the center of the pupil while the opposite eye is central.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common mode of inheritance of isolated congenital cataracts?
pool.rationale: Most heritable congenital cataracts are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Autosomal recessive and X-linked inheritance patterns can occur but these are less common.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What ophthalmic disorder is moyamoya disease associated with?

options.b: CHARGE syndrome (coloboma, heart defects, choanal atresia, mental retardation, genitourinary abnormalities, and ear abnormalities)

pool.rationale: Morning-glory disc anomaly has been associated with basal encephalocele in patients with midfacial anomalies, PHACE syndrome (posterior fossa malformations, hemangiomas, arterial lesions, cardiac and eye anomalies), and abnormalities of the carotid circulation, including moyamoya disease.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 1-year-old child presents for evaluation of constant, large-angle exotropia that has been present since birth. Aside from a complete ophthalmic examination, what additional piece of information is crucial to obtain?
pool.rationale:
Infantile exotropia (XT) presents before age 6 months with a large-angle, constant exodeviation. Patients who are otherwise healthy (no ocular or systemic disease) are classified as primary infantile XT. However, one must consider secondary causes, as patients with infantile XT are at increased risk of associated neurologic impairment or developmental delay. Referral for neurologic assessment may be necessary if there concerns about neurologic or developmental delay. As mentioned in the question stem, a complete ophthalmic exam, including a dilated fundus examination, is required in new patients with strabismus, as XT may also result from retinal or optic nerve abnormalities.
Monocular occlusion testing is helpful when evaluating patients with intermittent XT with more exodeviation at distance than near. Interpupillary distance, if large, can result in pseudoexotropia. Infantile XT is classically large angle (> 30 prism diopters) and difficult to mistake as pseudoexotropia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What oral medication is the most appropriate treatment for an infant with ophthalmia neonatorum secondary to Chlamydia trachomatis infection?
pool.rationale: Infants with Chlamydia trachomatis infection acquired at birth can present with papillary conjunctivitis during the first week of life. Although the eye disease is usually self-­limited, C trachomatis infection can cause pneumonia and otitis media in neonates. Therefore, systemic treatment with oral erythromycin is indicated.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What characteristic best distinguishes acquired nystagmus from congenital motor nystagmus (infantile nystagmus syndrome)?

options.c: exponential decrease in velocity of the slow phase
options.d: change in direction of the fast phase depending on which eye is fixating

pool.rationale: Oscillopsia is characteristic of nystagmus acquired in adulthood and is rare in CMN. Patients with congenital motor nystagmus (CMN; infantile nystagmus syndrome) often adopt an abnormal head position to take advantage of the better vision that is possible at a null point. An exponential decrease in velocity of the slow phase and a fast-phase direction that reverses with a change in fixation are characteristic of latent nystagmus (fusion maldevelopment nystagmus syndrome).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What surgical step is usually included in surgical treatment for esotropic Duane syndrome?

options.a: recession of the medial rectus on the affected side combined with resection of the lateral rectus on the affected side
options.b: resection of the lateral rectus on the affected side
options.c: resection of the lateral rectus on the unaffected side
options.d: recession of the medial rectus on the affected side

pool.rationale:
Duane retraction syndrome is a spectrum of ocular motility disorders characterized by anomalous co-contracture of the medial and lateral rectus muscles on actual or attempted adduction. It is caused by a hypoplastic or absent 6th cranial nerve with aberrant innervation to the lateral rectus muscle by the third cranial nerve. This leads to globe retraction on attempted adduction.
No surgery will fully normalize rotations in Duane syndrome due to innervational abnormalities. Therefore, surgery is reserved for primary position deviations, head turns, marked globe retraction, or large upshoots or downshoots.
Treatment of esotropic Duane syndrome is primarily recession of the medial rectus muscle on the affected side. The purpose of surgery in this situation is to expand the field of single binocular vision and reduce the head turn. Resection of the lateral rectus muscle in this case could induce further globe retraction, so resections are generally avoided in Duane syndrome.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Where is the origin of the superior oblique?
pool.rationale: The superior oblique originates from the orbital apex above the annulus of Zinn. It passes through the trochlea, which is the functional origin of the muscle. The inferior oblique originates from the orbital rim, and the remaining extraocular muscles originate from the annulus of Zinn.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A newborn infant is diagnosed with unilateral congenital cataract. Horizontal corneal diameters are 8 mm in the affected eye and 10 mm in the unaffected eye. What diagnosis should be considered?
pool.rationale: Persistent fetal vasculature (PFV, previously referred to as persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous or PHPV) is a congenital condition caused by the failure of the fetal hyaloid vasculature to regress properly. Clinically, there is almost always associated microcornea. Congenital glaucoma is associated with buphthalmos, or enlarged corneal diameters. In Coats disease, the corneal diameter is normal. In posterior lenticonus, the corneal diameter is normal.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What preoperative test would be most helpful in assessing the opportunity for single binocular vision after strabismus surgery?
pool.rationale: Determining the potential for postoperative single binocular vision is a vital component of the preoperative assessment for strabismus surgery. Although the cover-uncover test, the Hess screen, and the Lancaster red-green test are all helpful for measuring strabismic deviation, only the amblyoscope also tests for retinal correspondence. Another method of simulating the target postoperative alignment is by using prisms.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 5-month-old girl presents for evaluation of a large-angle exotropia and face turn that have been present since birth. What clinical feature can be seen in children with this type of strabismus?
pool.rationale:
Infantile exotropia is characterized by a large-angle outward deviation that is often associated with neurologic impairment or craniofacial disorders. Although the child may appear healthy, a careful developmental history is important, and referral for neurologic evaluation should be considered if there are indications of developmental delay.
High hyperopia is associated with accommodative esotropia.
Cross-fixation occurs in a large-angle esotropia with the use of the adducted eye for fixation of objects in the contralateral temporal field.
Convergence-retraction nystagmus is part of the dorsal midbrain syndrome, associated with paralysis of upward gaze, defective convergence, eyelid retraction, and pupillary light-near dissociation. With attempted upgaze, co-contraction of all the horizontal muscles occurs, and the eyes are pulled into the orbit. During this movement, the medial rectus muscles overpower the lateral rectus muscles, causing the eyes to converge.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Teller Acuity Cards II are likely to overestimate the vision in what eye condition?
pool.rationale: Strabismic amblyopia has features that differ from other types of amblyopia. Grating acuity, such as is tested with Teller Acuity Cards II and the LEA Grating Acuity Test, is reduced less than acuity measured with optotypes. Therefore, grating acuity can overestimate the vision. Linear LEA symbols, ETDRS (Early Treatment of Diabetic Retinopathy Study) charts, and crowded HOTV charts accurately measure visual acuity in strabismic amblyopia. In refractive and deprivational amblyopia, this effect is not seen. The presence of astigmatism does not affect the accuracy of grating acuity measurements.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What part of the visual system demonstrates abnormal neuronal development in amblyopia?
pool.rationale: Amblyopic visual deficits result primarily from visual cortical changes. With abnormal visual experience early in life, cells of the primary visual cortex can lose their ability to respond to stimulation of 1 or both eyes, and the cells that remain responsive show significant functional deficiencies, including abnormally large receptive fields. Visual cortex deficiencies may account for the crowding phenomenon, in which optotypes are easier to recognize when isolated than when surrounded by similar forms. Abnormalities are also found in neurons within the lateral geniculate body, but the retina in amblyopia is essentially normal. Amblyopia is primarily a defect of central vision; the peripheral visual field is usually normal.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What cause of leukocoria is associated with microphthalmos?
pool.rationale: Each of the answer choices (Coats disease, retinoblastoma, persistent fetal vasculature, and Toxocara species) can cause unilateral leukocoria. However, only persistent fetal vasculature is associated with microphthalmos. Additionally, it is associated with elongated ciliary processes, cataract, retinal detachment, and angle-closure glaucoma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: When is the most rapid rate of growth in the axial length of the eye postnatally?
pool.rationale: In a human newborn, the average axial length of the eye is 14.5-15.5 mm. The majority of growth of the axial length occurs in the first year of life, increasing by approximately 4 mm in the first 6 months and 2 mm in the subsequent 6 months. The final axial length is reached when the individual is 13 to 16 years old. The average axial length in an adult is 23-24 mm.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Pediatric Ophthalmology & Strabismus — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A parent brings a child to the clinic for evaluation of strabismus. What finding on examination would suggest the strabismus is longstanding?
pool.rationale:
Anomalous retinal correspondence (ARC) occurs when the fovea of the fixating eye has acquired a visual direction in common with a peripheral retinal element in the deviated eye. This is an adaptive mechanism that takes time to develop; therefore, a short history of esotropia would not be associated with ARC. ARC would not develop with decreased vision in one eye in the absence of strabismus. An exophoria would not be associated with ARC, since the eyes are not deviated under binocular conditions.

pool.q: A 4-year-old child presents with conjunctival injection and fever. He also notably has a swollen tongue, swollen hands, and enlarged cervical lymph nodes. What extraocular evaluation is most urgently indicated?
pool.rationale: The most significant complication of Kawasaki disease is coronary artery aneurysm. Coronary artery evaluation by 2-dimensional echocardiography is, therefore, warranted upon diagnosing Kawasaki disease. Kawasaki disease is a febrile illness primarily affecting children younger than 5 years. The cause is unknown. Abnormalities include unexplainable fever lasting 5 or more days; bilateral conjunctival injection; mucous membrane changes of injected or fissured lips, injected pharynx, or "strawberry tongue" extremity changes involving erythema of the palms or soles, edema of the hands or feet, or generalized or periungual desquamation; rash; and cervical lymphadenopathy. Beside conjunctivitis, the next most common ocular finding is anterior uveitis that is generally self-limited. Rare ocular findings can include keratitis, papilledema, optic neuritis, and subconjunctival hemorrhage.

pool.q: When operating on the inferior oblique muscle, damage to the associated nerve can cause what unwanted side effect?
pool.rationale: The nerve to the inferior oblique carries the pupillary parasympathetic fibers; damage to this structure can cause an enlarged pupil. Anterior segment ischemia occurs when more than 2 rectus muscles are operated on at once, as they carry much of the blood supply to the anterior segment; the oblique muscles do not carry any blood to the anterior segment. Strabismus surgery on the inferior rectus muscle frequently causes widening or narrowing of the palpebral fissure because of that muscle's fascial attachments to the lower lid; the inferior oblique does not have similar attachments. The nerves to the lacrimal gland are not typically encountered during strabismus surgery.

pool.q: Patients with pseudoxanthoma elasticum have a higher incidence of what ocular finding?
pool.rationale:
Pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE) is an autosomal recessive disease characterized by fragmentation of elastic fibers commonly affecting skin, blood vessels, and eyes. Patients may present with small papular lesions of the axilla, neck, and groin. These skin regions may also have laxity ("chicken neck"). Other complications include gastrointestinal bleeding, premature atherosclerosis, and myocardial infarction. Ocular manifestations include angioid streaks and a dimpling of Bruch membrane causing a peau d’orange (orange peel) fundus appearance.
Patients with pseudoxanthoma elasticum have a higher incidence of disc drusen. Disc drusen are often inherited from the patient’s parents and appear in the first couple of decades of life. Disc drusen may appear as refractile gray-yellow bodies if near the surface of the nerve. However, often they are buried and not clinically visible. One useful clinical finding often seen with disc drusen is anomalous branching of the large retinal vessels over the disc. Rare complications of disc drusen include subretinal neovascular membrane or hemorrhage. B scan ultrasonography and computed tomography are useful imaging tools to identify disc drusen.

pool.q: What is the most appropriate method of visual acuity testing in a typical 3- to 4-year-old child?

options.a: HOTV testing, and if unable, follow with Snellen acuity testing
options.b: HOTV testing, and if unable, follow with LEA symbol testing
options.c: Snellen acuity testing, and if unable, follow with differential objection to cover testing
options.d: Snellen acuity testing, and if unable, follow with Teller acuity testing

pool.rationale: Visual acuity testing is dependent upon age and whether the child knows the letters of the alphabet. The Snellen acuity test is the gold standard, but in children ages 2 to 5, matching tests such as the HOTV and LEA symbols might be cognitively easier. Teller acuity testing is typically reserved for preverbal infants, or children with cognitive and verbal delays.

pool.q: For a 7-year-old child with orbital cellulitis, what would be the most likely characteristic of the causative source?
pool.rationale: Most young children with orbital cellulitis have infections caused by a single aerobic pathogen. In the neonate, S aureus and gram-negative bacilli are most common. In older children and adults, S aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, and S pneumoniae are common etiologic agents. Concurrent infections with multiple pathogens, including gram-negative and anaerobic organisms, can occur in older or immunosuppressed patients.

pool.q: What is the most likely diagnosis in an infant with decreased vision and paradoxical pupillary responses?
pool.rationale:
Paradoxical pupils, a pupillary constriction in response to darkness, are most commonly associated with retinal dystrophies, although they can occur with optic neuropathies.
Amblyopia is a unilateral, or less commonly, a bilateral reduction of best-corrected visual acuity that cannot be attributed directly to the effect of any structural abnormality of the eye or visual pathways. Subtle afferent pupillary defects occur rarely and only in severe cases of amblyopia, not a paradoxical pupillary response.
Delayed visual maturation (DVM) is the condition wherein normal visual fixation and tracking do not develop in an infant within the first 3 months of life.
Cortical or cerebral visual impairment (CVI) is a condition in which visual deficits result from pathology posterior to the lateral geniculate nucleus. They usually have normal pupillary responses.

pool.q: What nerve typically provides aberrant innervation to the levator in Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome?
pool.rationale: Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome is the result of a congenital trigemino-oculomotor synkinesis of the jaw and levator muscles. The motor division of the trigeminal nerve aberrantly provides innervation in this scenario. The ptotic eyelid elevates with opening of the mouth or movement of the jaw to the contralateral side.

pool.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with recent onset intermittent exotropia and is found to have a cycloplegic refraction of +5.50 D sphere OD and OS. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.a: correction of full cycloplegic refractive error and vision therapy
options.b: correction of full cycloplegic refractive error
options.c: correction of refractive error with overminus lenses
options.d: correction of full cycloplegic refractive error and base-in prisms

pool.rationale:
Intermittent exotropia is characterized by a variable outward drifting of an eye when fusional factors become disrupted. Most often this condition becomes manifest during times of inattention, fatigue, or stress. Because equal and appropriate visual acuity helps maintain fusion, with a decrease in the ability to accommodate and compensate for an underlying latent hyperopia, some patients with more than 4.0 D of uncorrected hyperopia may gain better control of the exodeviation after optical correction. Mild-to-moderate hyperopia would not routinely be corrected.
As the visual acuity of this patient is currently unknown, the first management step would be to correct the refractive error. Vision therapy with active orthoptic exercises could be instituted but might not be necessary. For some cases, overcorrection of myopia by 2.00 D to 4.00 D can stimulate accommodative convergence to help control the exodeviation. However, the patient in this case is hyperopic.
Base-in prisms might also be used if there is any residual angle despite glasses, but typically only in those patients who might not be surgical candidates for correction of any residual deviation.

pool.q: A 13-year-old patient presents with bilateral vision loss, pain with eye movement, and bilateral optic disc swelling. What finding is most predictive of future risk for multiple sclerosis (MS)?
pool.rationale: Pediatric patients are more likely than adults to present with papillitis rather than retrobulbar optic neuritis, and bilateral disease also is more common. Younger children are especially likely to have bilateral disease, although it can occur in teens as well. While older age at presentation confers greater risk for future MS, it is the presence of white matter lesions on brain MRI, as in adults, that is the most important risk factor. Laterality is not an independent risk factor, nor is a viral illness preceding the optic neuritis.

pool.q: A 2-month-old infant has an enlarging hemangioma of an upper eyelid and orbit, with anisometropic astigmatism and secondary blepharoptosis. What is the preferred primary treatment for this patient?
pool.rationale: Although all the listed treatments can be effective for some hemangiomas, oral propranolol is now preferred for the treatment of vision-threatening periocular hemangiomas. Topical timolol can be an effective treatment for superficial hemangiomas, but not for orbital lesions.

pool.q: A premature infant born at 34 weeks and weighing 1100 grams has microcephaly, intraventricular calcifications, and bilateral retinitis. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
pool.rationale: Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is an acquired congenital infection, most commonly causing disease in immunocompromised and ill infants. Congenital CMV disease is characterized by intraventricular calcifications, microcephaly, fever, jaundice, hearing loss, retinitis, optic nerve abnormalities, microphthalmos, cataract, and uveitis. The retinal inflammation is characterized by retinal whitening, edema, perivascular sheathing, and intraretinal hemorrhages. The mainstay treatment for sight-threatening congenital CMV is antiviral therapy such as ganciclovir. Intravenous (IV) penicillin G is treatment for syphilis, IV prednisolone would be treatment for noninfectious disease, and IV vancomycin is an antibiotic for bacterial disease.

pool.q: What congenital iris abnormality represents a sequestration of epithelium during embryologic development?

options.a: cyst of the iris pigment epithelium

pool.rationale:
Iris stromal cysts are enlarging congenital lesions that are caused by sequestration of epithelial tissues during embryogenesis. Due to enlargement, they may cause visual obstruction, glaucoma, and corneal decompensation.
Cysts of the iris pigment epithelium are caused by separation of the 2 layers of the iris pigment epithelium, not by sequestration of tissue. They typically are stable and do not usually cause clinical complications. Pigment epithelial cysts at the pupil border, also referred to as central cysts, can be hereditary. Although they sometimes enlarge slowly, they rarely cause complications. Lisch nodules are hamartomas of the iris that are present in patients with neurofibromatosis type 1.

pool.q: A 26-year-old woman has had 3 years of diplopia. She had an eye injury 5 years ago. Her best corrected visual acuity is 20/20 OD, 20/400 OS. Examination reveals a 40 prism-diopter left exotropia with a slight adduction deficit. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Sensory exotropia develops in the setting of significant visual loss in one eye. The exotropia can develop years after the vision loss, and if it occurs in older children or adults it can be associated with diplopia. A small adduction deficit can be present.
Medial rectus entrapment is relatively uncommon, and it would typically present with strabismus soon after the injury, not years later. Myasthenia gravis and thyroid eye disease can both present with a large-angle exotropia, but they would not be expected to be associated with visual decrease.

pool.q: Epiblepharon is a congenital anomaly of the eyelid characterized by what anatomical findings?

options.a: horizontal fold of skin adjacent to the lower eyelid, causing inward rotation of the lashes against the cornea
options.b: crescent-shaped fold of skin running vertically between the eyelids and overlying the inner canthus
options.c: eversion of the eyelid margin secondary to a vertical deficiency of the skin
options.d: enlargement of the lateral aspect of the palpebral fissure, with downward displacement of a temporal half of the lower eyelid

pool.rationale:
Epiblepharon is a congenital anomaly in which a horizontal fold of skin adjacent to either the upper or lower eyelid—most commonly, the lower eyelid—may rotate the lashes inward against the cornea, as shown. The eyelid margin is in normal height with respect to the globe. The eyelashes are noted to be rubbing against the conjunctiva and cornea; however, the cornea tends to tolerate this condition well, and it is often minimally symptomatic. The condition tends to occur more frequently in chubby-cheeked and Asian infants. Unlike congenital entropion, epiblepharon often resolves spontaneously in the first 2 years of life. Cases that do not resolve or that cause chronic corneal irritation require surgical repair. The crescent-shaped fold of skin running vertically between the eyelids and overlying the inner canthus is the epicanthus. The eversion of the eyelid margin secondary to a vertical deficiency of the skin is congenital ectropion. Euryblepharon is enlargement of the lateral aspect of the palpebral fissure, with downward displacement of a temporal half of the lower eyelid.

pool.q: A 6-month-old child presents with poor vision and searching nystagmus. The child has at least light perception vision but is unable to fixate or follow lighted objects. If the visual acuity could be measured, what vision level would the child most likely have?
pool.rationale: Searching nystagmus suggests that the child has poor vision, worse than 20/200. Pendular nystagmus typically occurs in patients with visual acuity better than 20/200 in at least 1 eye. Jerk nystagmus often is associated with visual acuity between 20/60 and 20/100.

pool.q: What condition is associated with an abnormally high number of crossed fibers in the optic chiasm?
pool.rationale: Ocular albinism is associated with iris transillumination, foveal aplasia or hypoplasia, and decreased retinal pigmentation. Both human and animal studies have shown an abnormally high number of crossed fibers in the optic chiasm, which precludes stereopsis and is associated with strabismus. Optic nerve hypoplasia and morning glory disc are not associated with abnormalities in the crossed fibers of the optic chiasm. Achromatopsia is not typically associated with optic nerve abnormalities.

pool.q: What is the most common antimetabolite used to treat uveitis in children?
pool.rationale: Azathioprine, methotrexate, and mycophenolate mofetil are all antimetabolites that can be used to treat uveitis in children. Methotrexate is most commonly used, and numerous studies have shown its efficacy in treating both arthritis and uveitis in children. Etanercept is not an antimetabolite. It is a TNF-alpha inhibitor that should be avoided in the treatment of uveitis because it may cause inflammatory ocular disease.

pool.q: An 18-month-old boy who underwent bilateral nasolacrimal duct probing 6 months ago presents with recurrent epiphora and mucopurulent discharge from each eye. What is the most appropriate management?
pool.rationale:
Nasolacrimal duct (NLD) probing is indicated for congenital NLD obstruction that fails to resolve with age and conservative treatment, for a dacryocystocele in the newborn that is unresponsive to massage, and for previously failed NLD probing procedures. NLD probing is performed by passing Bowman probes of appropriate sizes through the canaliculus into the nasolacrimal sac, and then down the nasolacrimal duct into the nose. The patency of the NLD system is confirmed by metal-on-metal contact in the nose, as illustrated, and/or by successful irrigation of fluorescein solution into the nasopharynx. Infracture of the inferior turbinate is often performed in addition to the probing. Some surgeons employ balloon catheter dilation, intubation, or nasal endoscopy during the first surgery for NLD obstruction, but most reserve their use for patients who require a second procedure, as does the patient in this case.
Lacrimal massage is not typically useful for NLD obstruction that has already failed an initial probing. Dacryocystorhinostomy is a final option when NLD obstruction persists or recurs following the previously described procedures, and therefore is not yet indicated for this patient. Imaging studies such as dacryocystography are impractical in most instances and consequently are not required for diagnosing NLD obstruction.

pool.q: What additional eye motility abnormality do patients with infantile esotropia commonly have?

options.b: symmetric smooth pursuit in horizontal gaze

pool.rationale: DVD is associated with infantile esotropia. Vertical nystagmus and ocular flutter are not. Patients with infantile esotropia have asymmetric smooth pursuit, which is better in the temporal-to-nasal direction.

pool.q: What systemic condition is associated with microspherophakia?
pool.rationale:
Weill-Marchesani syndrome is associated with short status, stocky body habitus, brachydactyly (short fingers and toes), and microspherophakia.
Homocystinuria, hyperlysinemia, and sulfite oxidase deficiency are all associated with mental retardation. Patients with these conditions can develop ectopia lentis.

pool.q: What additional factors should be taken into account when selecting an intraocular lens for a small child undergoing cataract surgery?

options.a: The target refraction must account for the typical myopic shift that occurs with growth.
options.b: The target refraction must account for the typical hyperopic shift that occurs with growth.
options.c: The most refractive change happens in the second decade with puberty.
options.d: The final refractive outcome can be calculated based on age and the initial refractive status.

pool.rationale:
Because the child's eye continues to elongate throughout the first decade and beyond, the selection of an appropriate IOL power is complicated. Most surgeons implant IOLs with powers that children are anticipated to require in adulthood. These children can be expected to become progressively more myopic with time.
Studies have shown that in aphakic pediatric eyes, a variable myopic shift in refractive error of approximately 7.00–8.00 D occurs from 1 year to 10 years of age, with a wide standard deviation. This suggests that if a child is made emmetropic with an IOL at 1 year of age, refractive error at 10 years of age can be –8.00 D or greater. Target refraction also takes into consideration the fellow eye, and the risk of amblyopia.

pool.q: A 32-year-old man has bilateral vestibular schwannomas found during evaluation for hearing loss. He has decreased vision OS with a left relative afferent pupillary defect and swollen left optic nerve. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan is likely to show what additional abnormality?

options.a: bulbous enlargement of the intracranial left optic nerve
options.b: calcification of the optic radiations and chiasm
options.c: enhancement and thickening of the left optic nerve sheath
options.d: extraocular muscle enlargement and left orbital apex crowding

pool.rationale:
This patient most likely has an underlying diagnosis of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2), suggested by bilateral vestibular schwannomas. In this disease, optic nerve sheath meningioma is a common reason for adult-onset optic neuropathy, described best on MRI as enhancement and thickening of the optic nerve sheath.
Extraocular muscle enlargement and orbital apex crowding is more characteristic of thyroid eye disease with compressive optic neuropathy, which can present with optic nerve edema but is not as likely to be the responsible etiology of optic disc edema in a patient with NF2.
Bulbous enlargement of the intracranial left optic nerve describes optic pathway glioma, found in 20% of patients with neurofibromatosis type 1. It usually presents in childhood, not young adulthood.
Due to the posterior location of the optic radiations and chiasm, their calcification would not produce optic disc edema, unless they exert a significant mass effect, which would more typically produce papilledema (bilateral disc edema from increased intracranial pressure). There is a wide differential diagnosis of calcifications; one example is calcified intracranial astrocytic hamartoma from tuberous sclerosis.

pool.q: What is the typical range of visual acuity for a person with Leber congenital amaurosis?
pool.rationale: Leber congenital amaurosis is a retinal disease associated with severe vision loss in infancy, nystagmus, poor pupillary responses, and high hyperopia. Visual acuity is 20/200 or worse. A visual acuity of 20/100 or better would be atypical and suggest a different diagnosis.

pool.q: A child has experienced a stable, large-angle left exotropia and hypotropia with left ptosis since birth. The lid fissure widens in right gaze. What is the most likely etiology?
pool.rationale:
A third cranial nerve palsy is characterized by paralysis of the medial rectus, inferior oblique, superior rectus, inferior rectus, and levator muscles. This results in limitation to adduction, elevation, and depression, as well as in ptosis and fixed, dilated pupil. Because sixth and fourth cranial nerve function is maintained, the eye with third cranial nerve palsy is typically found exotropic and depressed. Signs of aberrant regeneration, which suggest a congenital abnormality, include widening of the lid fissure on attempted adduction.
Typically, a brainstem lesion presents as a more acute process, thus not demonstrating signs of aberrant regeneration. Congenital ptosis would not have the motility abnormality. In type 2 Duane syndrome the main limitation is adduction, but there is also some limitation to abduction. However, the lid-fissure narrowing on adduction is secondary to globe retraction, rather than aberrant innervation into the levator.

pool.q: What would be the preferred surgical treatment to treat the exodeviation from a sensory exotropia caused by a macular scar in the right eye?

options.a: lateral rectus recession and medial rectus resection in the left eye
options.c: lateral rectus recession and medial rectus resection in the right eye

This reduces the risk to the dominant eye from the complications of strabismus surgery, which include globe perforation or ocular ischemia. In this case, the right eye is the nondominant eye because of the macular scar.

pool.q: An infant recently diagnosed with juvenile xanthogranuloma based on skin biopsy and presence of iris nodules is found not to have neurofibromatosis. What can you tell the parents about the progression and prognosis of this condition?

options.a: Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a progressive condition that will require ongoing treatment until early adulthood.
options.b: Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a self-limited condition that usually resolves spontaneously by the age of 5 years.
options.c: Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a stable condition that can flare up in adulthood.
options.d: Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a self-limited condition that begins to resolve in early adulthood.

pool.rationale:
Juvenile xanthogranuloma (JXG) is a nonneoplastic histiocytic proliferation.
It develops in children younger than 2 years and is characterized by Touton giant cells. Skin involvement is usually present and consists of small, round orange-tan papules. Iris lesions are relatively rare and almost always unilateral. The iris lesions are fleshy yellow-brown masses and may be small and localized or diffusely infiltrate the iris, resulting in heterochromia. Hyphema secondary to spontaneous bleeding is a characteristic clinical presentation. Children at greatest risk for ocular involvement are those with multiple skin lesions, and they are at risk of developing secondary glaucoma, presenting with pain, acute vision loss, and photophobia.
JXG is a self-limited condition that usually resolves spontaneously by age 5 years.

pool.q: What is a characteristic of trichotillomania on slit lamp examination?
pool.rationale: Trichotillomania is characterized by the pulling out of one’s hair, frequently including the eyebrows and eyelashes. The characteristic appearance includes madarosis, broken hairs, and regrowth of hairs of varying lengths. Distichiasis is the presence of an accessory row of eyelashes growing out of or slightly posterior to the meibomian gland orifices. Epiblepharon is a congenital horizontal fold of skin, typically of the lower lid, that turns the lashes inward against the cornea.

pool.q: A 30-year-old man presents for evaluation of “one eye turning out” when he is tired. He has experienced this for several years. Initial evaluation demonstrates orthophoria. Upon cover testing, an exodeviation becomes present, although he is able to resume fusion with blinking. How is his exodeviation most accurately described?
pool.rationale: This is a case of intermittent exotropia. The grading of control of an intermittent exotropia is usually classified as poor, fair, or good. The patient is initially orthophoric, and by history also has periods of orthophoric alignment. The exotropia becomes manifest after disruption of fusion with cover testing, and fusion can be resumed with blinking, which indicates fair control. Poor control of an intermittent exotropia is indicated by periods of prolonged manifest exotropia occurring spontaneously, while good control is indicated by an exodeviation that is manifested only by cover testing and in which fusion can rapidly be regained without blinking or refixating. An exophoria would be suggested by an exodeviation that is present only with complete disruption of binocular vision (eg, alternate cover test).

pool.q: The results of a cycloplegic retinoscopy in an otherwise healthy, asymptomatic 3-year-old child are likely to reveal what approximate refractive error?
pool.rationale:
A 3-year-old child is expected to have some hyperopia, approximately between 2 and 3 diopters. Infants are hyperopic and can become slightly more hyperopic until about 7 years of age. Then the refraction shifts toward plano until about age 16, during a process called emmetropization. If myopia presents before age 10, increased myopia (6.0 D or more) has a greater likelihood of developing. Low amounts of astigmatism are common in infants and can resolve, but it is most likely with-the-rule astigmatism in children. Anisometropia is amblyogenic.

pool.q: At what age should an infant be able to maintain fixation and react with facial expressions?
pool.rationale: Although there is some variability, the nervous system is typically mature enough at age 6–8 weeks for an infant to maintain visual fixation and react with facial expressions. Infants aged 2–3 months should be interested in bright objects. By age 3–4 months, the nasal bias for smooth pursuit should have resolved, the eyes should be orthotropic, and fix-and-follow responses to a small (2–4 inches in diameter) toy should be present.

pool.q: A 4-year-old child is referred for failed vision screening. The acuity is 20/60 right eye and 20/20 left eye. Retinoscopy demonstrates a -4.00 refractive error of the right eye. On slit-lamp examination there is a central nuclear oil droplet cataract of the right eye. Fundoscopy easily demonstrates a normal-appearing optic nerve and retina. The ophthalmologist prescribes glasses, and the child returns in 3 months. Visual acuity in the right eye is now 20/50. What is the next step in the management of this child?

options.b: daily atropine in the right eye to allow for vision outside the cataract
options.d: part-time patching of the left eye

pool.rationale: Amblyopia is diagnosed when a patient has a condition known to cause amblyopia and has decreased vision that cannot be fully explained by physical abnormities of the eye. Amblyopia sometimes coexists with vision loss associated with a structural defect. In this case, the central nuclear oil droplet cataract has caused anisometropic myopia. Thus, in order to determine the extent of visual impairment from anisometropic amblyopia rather than the cataract, a trial of amblyopia treatment with patching is the next appropriate step.

pool.q: Short palpebral fissures, telecanthus, epicanthus, ptosis, microphthalmia, and esotropia are classic for what syndrome?
pool.rationale:
The classic ocular features of fetal alcohol syndrome are short palpebral fissures, telecanthus, epicanthus, ptosis, microphthalmia, and esotropia.
Goldenhar patients have hemifacial microsomia. Ocular abnormalities include epibulbar dermoids, dermolipomas, eyelid colobomas, microphthalmia, cataract, and iris abnormalities. Also, Duane retraction syndrome is more common in patients with Goldenhar syndrome.
Treacher Collins syndrome is caused by the underdevelopment and sometimes agenesis of the zygoma and malar eminences. The lateral orbital rims are depressed, and the palpebral fissures slant downward because of lateral canthal dystopia.
Saethre-Chotzen syndrome is a mild craniosynostosis syndrome that may present with facial asymmetry. Ptosis is a common feature.

pool.q: In a patient who has an amblyopic eye with 20/400 vision and eccentric fixation, what is the best method to measure the amount of ocular misalignment?
pool.rationale: The Krimsky test does not rely on a sensory or motor response from the patient. Motor test results will not be accurate if there is eccentric fixation. pool.q: For acquired esotropia, the maximal angle of strabismus and fusional potential can be assessed by what test?

pool.q: What is the typical dissociated strabismus pattern seen in dissociated horizontal deviation?

options.b: a predominantly unilateral exodeviation with lesser torsional and vertical components
options.c: a predominantly unilateral esodeviation with lesser torsional and vertical components
options.d: a small unilateral exodeviation with a larger vertical component

pool.q: A 29-year-old woman with longstanding insulin-dependent diabetes has a 9-pound baby boy. This history increases the risk of what optic nerve condition?

Congenital glaucoma, iris coloboma, and retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) are not known defects stemming from insulin-dependent diabetes. pool.q: What congenital ocular disorder is most commonly associated with paradoxical pupillary reaction?

pool.q: What is the average axial length of the human eye in a newborn?
pool.rationale: The average axial length of the human eye in a newborn is 14.5-15.5 mm. The majority of growth of the axial length occurs in the first year of life; it increases by approximately 4 mm in the first 6 months of life and an additional 2 mm during the subsequent 6 months. The axial length reaches its final axial length when the individual is between the ages of 13 and 16 years. The average axial length in an adult is 23-24 mm.

pool.q: What ocular motor dysfunction will result in a V pattern strabismus?

A 6th nerve palsy would be expected to have an incomitant esotropia without a pattern. Duane syndrome type 1 would result in an incomitant esotropia due to limited abduction. pool.q: In addition to sporadic inheritance, what inheritance pattern is commonly associated with blepharophimosis-ptosis-epicanthus inversus syndrome?

pool.q: What is an example of a comitant deviation?

options.c: Duane syndrome of the left eye

pool.q: A child with uncorrected infantile esotropia and manifest latent nystagmus has a face turn to the left. This head posture is most likely related to what?
pool.rationale: Latent nystagmus occurs in children who have decreased fusion from early onset strabismus. When one eye is occluded, a jerk nystagmus develops in both eyes with the fast phase directed toward the uncovered eye. The null point is with the fixating eye in adduction. Latent nystagmus becomes manifest when both eyes are open but only 1 eye is being used for vision. Thus, in a child with manifest latent nystagmus, on fixation with the left eye, the null zone would be on adduction leading to a face turn to the left.

pool.q: What material are the extraocular muscle pulleys primarily composed of?
pool.rationale: Elastin is one component of the pulley; the others are smooth muscle and collagen. Striated muscle, hyaluronic acid, and chondroitin sulfate are not known constituents of the pulleys.

pool.q: What category of congenital anomaly is represented by a choroidal coloboma?
pool.rationale: Dysraphism represents a failure to fuse. Agenesis represents developmental failure, as is found in anophthalmia, whereas hypoplasia is due to developmental arrest, such as in optic nerve hypoplasia. Developmental excess such as that seen with distichiasis is the cause of hyperplasia.

pool.q: What procedure is effective at simultaneously treating dissociated vertical deviation and inferior oblique overaction?
pool.rationale:
Dissociated vertical deviation (DVD) is an innervational disorder in which either eye slowly drifts upward and outward with extortion when the eye is occluded or there is visual inattention. It typically develops by age 2 years and is commonly associated with infantile strabismus, typically esotropia or exotropia (50%). Treatment of DVD is indicated when the deviation is noticeable (more than 6–8 prism diopters) or is present frequently during the day. Treatments include optical penalization for unilateral or highly asymmetric bilateral DVD or vertical muscle surgery.
Large superior rectus muscle recessions can be effective at treating DVD, titrated based on the amount of the hypertropia and the symmetry of the DVD. Inferior rectus muscle resection or plication can help treat residual DVD. In cases of DVD and inferior oblique overaction, inferior oblique muscle anterior transposition has been shown to be effective. Inferior oblique myectomy is effective at treating inferior oblique overaction without DVD.

pool.q: In what situation is a posterior capsulorrhexis at the time of pediatric cataract surgery indicated?

options.c: in the presence of zonular laxity
options.d: when a Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy can be performed at a later date

The younger the child, the higher the risk of PCO. A posterior capsulorrhexis at the time of cataract surgery is not indicated in older children or in those who can undergo a YAG capsulotomy when indicated. An anterior capsulorrhexis is an important step in pediatric surgery but does not determine whether posterior capsulorrhexis is needed. An anterior vitrectomy is generally performed with posterior capsulorrhexis in young patients to decrease the incidence of visually significant fibrous membrane development.

pool.q: A patient is diagnosed with pseudopapilledema. What frequently found additional ophthalmic finding supports this diagnosis?

pool.q: A patient has an electroretinography (ERG) result showing an extinguished photopic response. Specialized ERG testing shows normal function of the blue (short-wavelength) cones. What is the inheritance pattern of this disorder?

pool.q: What is the most common outcome when a needle perforates the sclera during strabismus surgery?

In most cases, scleral perforation results in a chorioretinal scar. Most perforations go unrecognized unless specifically investigated by indirect ophthalmoscopy. If vitreous escapes through the perforation, many surgeons will apply immediate cryotherapy or laser to the area. Topical antibiotics are usually given postoperatively when a perforation is recognized. Referral to a retina specialist is appropriate.
Perforation can result in vitreous hemorrhage, endophthalmitis, and retinal detachment, but these complications are less frequent.

pool.q: A patient undergoes surgery to repair an orbital floor fracture and free an entrapped inferior rectus muscle. Postoperatively, a hypotropia is present and persists for 6 months following the surgery. What surgery is most likely to provide benefit at this time?
pool.rationale: Despite the repair of the orbital floor and release of the entrapped muscle, restriction can persist. Re-exploration of the fracture will then not be of benefit. In these cases, recession of the restricted muscle is the next step. An inferior rectus recession is indicated in this case. A superior rectus resection may be done if the inferior rectus recession results in undercorrection. A transposition could be considered for a muscle palsy, but an inferior rectus muscle palsy would result in a hypertropia, not a hypotropia.

pool.q: Möbius syndrome is characterized by the association of hypoplasia of cranial nerve VI and what other feature?

pool.q: In relation to normal eyelid structures, where is a dacryocystocele usually located?

pool.q: What is the inheritance pattern for ectopia lentis et pupillae?
pool.rationale:
Ectopia lentis et pupillae is a rare, autosomal recessive condition. Pertinent clinical features include bilaterally displaced pupils, usually inferotemporally, with lens dislocation in the opposite direction of the displaced pupil. Ectopia lentis et pupillae may be the result of membranes extending from a posterior origin to attach to the proximal pupil margin. The figures show these findings. The membranes are believed to cause traction of the iris toward the membranes (resulting in the iris abnormality) and disruption of the zonules (resulting in lens subluxation in the opposite direction). Affected patients have microspherophakia, miosis, and poor pupillary dilation with mydriatics. Lens dislocation causes decreased visual acuity, making spectacle correction essential. High myopia secondary to axial globe elongation has been reported. Aphakic correction is often needed, depending on the degree of lens dislocation. Amblyopia is the main complication and is managed by refractive correction and occlusion therapy. Lensectomy may result in retinal detachment or vitreous hemorrhage. High-frequency ultrasound preoperatively may allow assessment of risk or retinal detachment or vitreous hemorrhage. Ectopia lentis et pupillae is nonprogressive.

pool.q: An ophthalmologist is measuring the misalignment of the eyes of a patient with strabismus. As the patient changes the fixating eye, the amount of misalignment measured differs significantly. What type of strabismus is this?
pool.rationale:
Hering's law states that yoke muscles receive equal and simultaneous innervation during gaze. In the case of restrictive and paralytic muscles, the abnormal response of one of the yoke muscles causes the angle of deviation to vary, depending on the fixating eye. The extra innervation required to move the restricted or paralytic eye is shared by the unaffected eye, causing excessive action of the yoke muscle and a greater angle of deviation. When the unaffected eye is fixating, the amount of misalignment is known as the primary deviation. When the restricted or paralytic eye is fixating, the amount of misalignment is known as the secondary deviation.
In infantile strabismus, comitant strabismus, and A-pattern strabismus, the yoke muscles contract normally, and the angle of deviation is not dependent on the fixating eye.

pool.q: What features might be found when evaluating the brain scan and cerebrospinal fluid of a child with idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri)?

options.a: enlarged ventricles and abnormal cerebrospinal fluid composition
options.b: normal-sized or small ventricles and abnormal cerebral fluid composition
options.c: normal-sized or small ventricles and normal cerebrospinal fluid composition
options.d: enlarged ventricles and normal cerebrospinal fluid composition

pool.rationale: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH), or pseudotumor cerebri, is characterized by an increase in intracranial pressure, normal-sized or small ventricles on neuroimaging and normal cerebrospinal fluid composition. IIH can occur in children of any age and has been associated with viral infections, drug use (tetracycline, corticosteroids, vitamin A, nalidixic acid, thyroid medications, growth hormone), and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Prepubescent children with IIH have a lower incidence of obesity compared with adult patients, and the male-to-female ratio is approximately equal. Postpubescent children with IIH have a clinical profile similar to that of adults, with a higher incidence of obesity compared with younger patients and female gender preponderance. Because IIH is a diagnosis of exclusion, findings that suggest another disorder, such as abnormal cerebrospinal fluid composition or enlarged ventricles, exclude the diagnosis.

pool.q: A 4-year-old child is discovered to have a visual acuity of 20/25 OD and 20/200 OS. What is the recommended initial management?
pool.rationale: Cycloplegic refraction is an important part of the evaluation of pediatric patients. Cycloplegia is necessary to paralyze accommodation and accurately determine refractive error. The recognition of significant refractive error is important in the diagnosis and treatment of amblyopia. Occlusion therapy, optical penalization, and prescription of prism lenses would not be appropriate until a workup including cycloplegic refraction was completed and the correct cause of amblyopia was determined.

pool.q: An infant born at 25 weeks' gestation is diagnosed with 3 clock hours of neovascularization in zone II with plus disease. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
pool.rationale:
Treatment of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) has progressed from the original use of cryotherapy to laser in the attempt to prevent neovascularization and retinal detachment. Treatment with laser now is recommended for prethreshold disease, based on the results of the Early Treatment of Retinopathy of Prematurity (ETROP) trial.
Originally, the Cryotherapy for Retinopathy of Prematurity (CRYO-ROP) trial defined threshold disease as 5 contiguous or 8 total clock hours of stage 3 ROP in zone I or II with plus disease.
The ETROP went further to define which infants with prethreshold disease would benefit from treatment, including those with zone I any stage ROP with plus disease, zone I stage 3 ROP without plus disease, and zone II stage 2 or 3 ROP with plus disease.
In this case, the baby met treatment criteria by having zone II stage 3 with plus disease.

pool.q: A frontalis suspension is most strongly indicated for what type of blepharoptosis?
pool.rationale: Frontalis suspension surgery is performed when levator function is poor or absent, to allow the frontalis muscle to lift the brow and elevate the eyelid. Congenital ptosis is characterized by decreased levator function, lid lag, and often absent or poorly formed upper eyelid crease due to dysgenesis of the levator muscle. Mechanical ptosis, involutional ptosis, and Horner syndrome involve normal levator function and would be suitable for levator advancement surgery.

pool.q: Galactosemia, if left untreated, will result in what ocular condition?
pool.rationale:
Galactosemia leads to the development of cataracts, typically with an "oil droplet" appearance. The cataracts may resolve with dietary restriction before a child is 4 months old. Because a lack of treatment leads to cataracts and intellectual deficiency, the ophthalmologist can play an important role in preventing these complications by helping to make the correct diagnosis.

pool.q: An individual with no prior history of strabismus was involved in a car accident and has had stable vertical diplopia for over 6 months. He has a right hypertropia that increases on left gaze and on right head tilt. Surgery has been recommended. What procedure would be the most appropriate?

options.a: recession of the right inferior oblique
options.b: resection of the right superior rectus
options.c: resection of the left inferior rectus
options.d: intrasheath tenectomy of the right superior oblique

pool.rationale: These findings are consistent with a diagnosis of a right superior oblique weakness, a right hypertropia, greater in left gaze and right head tilt. Surgery needs to address the primary deviation and also the muscle most involved in the field of action where the deviation is largest. In the absence of specific measurements, surgery needs to address the primary deviation. Only a right inferior oblique recession would lessen a right hypertropia. Resection of the left inferior rectus, resection of the right superior rectus, and a tenectomy of the right superior oblique would all worsen the right hypertropia.

pool.q: What term describes a greater than normal distance between the medial canthi?
pool.rationale:
Telecanthus is greater-than-normal distance between the medial canthi. This can be secondary to and present with hypertelorism, or it can be only a soft-tissue abnormality.
Hypertelorism is the excessive distance between the medial orbital walls and is detected radiographically.
Exorbitism is prominent eyes due to shallow orbits or an increased angle of divergence of the orbital walls.
In scaphocephaly, the skull is long in anterior-posterior axis and narrow bitemporally, usually from premature closure of the sagittal suture.

pool.q: A 4-year-old patient with +2.25 D of hyperopia in both eyes recently developed a small esotropia at distance and a large esotropia at near. What is the cause of her esotropia?

Patients with a high (AC/A) ratio esotropia have an excessive convergence response for the amount of accommodation required to focus while wearing their full cycloplegic correction. In this form of esotropia, the deviation is present only at near or is much larger at near. The refractive error in high AC/A ratio accommodative esotropia averages +2.25 D.
Refractive accommodative esotropia involves 3 factors: uncorrected hyperopia, accommodative convergence, and insufficient fusional divergence. Because of uncorrected hyperopia, the patient must accommodate to focus the retinal image. Accommodation is accompanied by the other components of the near reflex, namely convergence and miosis. If the patient's fusional divergence mechanism is insufficient to compensate for the increased convergence tonus, esotropia results. The angle of esotropia is approximately the same at distance and near fixation and is generally between 20 and 30 prism diopters. Patients with refractive accommodative esotropia have an average of +4.00 D of hyperopia.
Patients with divergence insufficiency esotropia show reduction in the angle of esotropia when wearing glasses but have a residual esotropia despite provision of the full hyperopic correction.
Congenital esotropia is another term for infantile esotropia, which is present by 6 months of age.

pool.q: The axial length of the eye of a newborn is approximately what percentage of its final adult size?

pool.q: What is the function of fusional convergence?
pool.rationale: Vergences are movements of the eyes in opposite directions. Fusional vergence is a motor response that serves to eliminate image disparity. Fusional convergence eliminates bitemporal retinal disparity and controls an exophoria. Fusional divergence eliminates binasal retinal disparity and controls an esophoria. Vertical fusional vergences are used to correct a hyperphoria.

pool.q: What is the preferred treatment to correct a compensatory head turn from nystagmus?

options.a: surgery to move the null point

pool.rationale:
A compensatory head turn is adapted to move the eyes to the null point. If a patient has a null point in right gaze, then they will turn their head to the left so that as they are walking or doing their activities, their eyes are in the null point and relatively stable, and their visual acuity is improved. Surgery or prisms can be used to decrease or eliminate the head turn by shifting the eyes so that the null point will be in primary position rather than in an eccentric gaze position.
Surgery is done to move the eyes in the direction of the head turn (another way of saying this is away from the direction of the gaze preference). Therefore, if the patient has a left head turn, the eyes are both surgically moved towards the left. In the Anderson procedure, this is done with medial rectus recession in one eye and lateral rectus recession in the other eye (in a left head turn, the surgeon would recess the medial rectus of the left eye and recess the lateral rectus of the right eye). In the Kestenbaum procedure (a recess-resect procedure), moving all 4 rectus muscles can be done to move the null point into primary position to correct the head turn (in a left head turn, for the left eye the surgeon would recess the medial rectus and resect the lateral rectus, while for the right eye the surgeon would resect the medial rectus and recess the lateral rectus).
Base-in prism will decrease the patient's drive for convergence, making nystagmus worse, may induce strabismus, and will not correct the head turn. Although base-in prism over both eyes is incorrect, prisms can be used in nystagmus to decrease head turn.  Prisms could be used to shift the perceived object location toward the null point, but this would require base-in prism over one eye and base-out prism over the other eye (eg, if left head turn and right-gaze null point, a base-out prism would be used over the left eye and a base-in prism over the right eye). Alternatively, if the patient has binocular fusion, bilateral base-out prisms can be used to induce convergence and dampen nystagmus. Prisms are sometimes used as a trial to predict surgical success.
Alternate patching therapy can make the nystagmus worse while patching because it can disrupt fusion and will not correct the head turn.
Pharmacologic therapy may be tried to decrease the nystagmus but will not affect the head turn.

pool.q: What orbital coherence tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings are most suggestive of orbital myositis?

options.d: thickening of the extraocular muscle belly with tendon involvement

Imaging studies show diffusely enlarged muscles with tendon involvement; the enlargement extends all the way to the insertion. This is in contrast to thyroid myopathy, where the tendon is spared.
A vascular orbital mass would suggest a hemangioma. Orbital fat stranding would be suggestive of orbital cellulitis.

pool.q: What is the most common presentation of retinoblastoma?
pool.rationale: The most common initial sign of retinoblastoma is leukocoria (white pupillary reflex), which is usually first noticed by the child's family and described as a glow, glint, or cat’s­ eye appearance. pool.q: A 16-year-old girl complains of eye fatigue, diplopia, and blurry vision with extended near work. Examination reveals no refractive error and no manifest strabismus. Convergence amplitudes are decreased and near point of convergence is remote. What intervention is recommended?
pool.rationale:
The question stem describes convergence insufficiency (CI). It is characterized by poor fusional convergence amplitudes and a remote near point of convergence. This sometimes results in symptoms of asthenopia, blurred near vision, and diplopia during near work, usually in older children or adults.
Treatment of symptomatic CI typically involves orthoptic exercises. Base-out prisms can be used to stimulate and strengthen fusional convergence amplitudes. Stereograms, pencil push ups, and computer-based or office-based convergence training programs are all viable options. If these exercises fail, base-in prism reading glasses may alleviate symptoms. Surgical treatment, usually medial rectus muscle resection, may be indicated in patients whose problems persist despite medical therapy.

pool.q: Pseudopapilledema is most frequently seen in patients with what type of refractive error?

options.a: thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) and free T4 levels

Therefore, a low platelet count would support the diagnosis. Hemangiomas would not affect thyroid hormone levels or red blood cell counts. pool.q: What family of disorder includes Bardet-Biedl syndrome, Senior-Løken syndrome, and Alström syndrome?
pool.rationale:
A ciliopathy is a disorder of cilia structure or function. Bardet-Biedl syndrome encompasses mutations on the proteins that mediate and regulate the microtubule-based intracellular transport process. Ciliopathies manifest as a constellation of features that include retinal degeneration, renal disease, and cerebral anomalies. The number of genes being identified with cilia dysfunction is increasing.

A larger amount of prism is then placed until the deviation no longer increases. pool.q: What type of uveitis is most common in children?

pool.q: What duction deficit and ocular misalignment best characterizes type 2 Duane retraction syndrome?
pool.rationale:
Duane retraction syndrome is a spectrum of ocular motility disorders characterized by anomalous co-contraction of the medial and lateral rectus muscles on actual or attempted adduction of the involved eye or eyes; this co-contraction causes the globe to retract. Horizontal eye movement can be limited to various degrees in both abduction and adduction.

Type 1, the most common form of Duane retraction syndrome, is defined as poor abduction and esotropia. A patient may adopt a head turn to establish binocular fusion, and the esotropia may be seen only in primary gaze or with a head turn to the opposite direction. Type 2 is defined by limited adduction and exotropia. Type 3 is defined as poor abduction and adduction; either esotropia or exotropia may result. Poor abduction should not result in an exotropia.

pool.q: A 5-year-old girl presents with a 1-month history of intermittent nasal discharge, tearing, itchy eyes, and conjunctival injection. What is the most appropriate therapy?
pool.rationale:
This patient presents with classic symptoms of seasonal allergies, including allergic conjunctivitis. The duration of these symptoms for 1 month, along with their intermittent nature makes viral conjunctivitis associated with a viral upper respiratory tract infection much less likely. Seasonal allergic conjunctivitis tends to occur in the spring and fall and is triggered by environmental contact with specific airborne allergens such as pollens from grasses, flowers, weeds, and trees. Patients typically present with reddened, watery eyes, boggy-appearing conjunctiva, and complaints of itchy eyes. Allergic shiners due to lower eyelid ecchymosis may also be present. Management of allergic conjunctivitis involves removal of the offending allergens from the patient's environment and systemic and/or topical medications. Oral antihistamines are the recommended systemic therapy. They tend to be less effective at relieving ocular symptoms, but are useful in cases where other symptoms, such as nasal congestion, are present. In addition, they are often better tolerated in children, because many children have an aversion to eyedrops. Cool compresses to the eyes can further increase patient comfort. Topical medications include mast-cell stabilizers, H1-receptor blockers, vasoconstrictors, anti-inflammatory agents, or combinations thereof.
Topical corticosteroid drops used in pulsed doses can effectively reduce allergic ocular symptoms, but should be reserved for severe cases, and patients need to be monitored closely for steroid adverse effects, such as cataracts or glaucoma. If scrapings of the conjunctiva are obtained in patients with allergic conjunctivitis, eosinophils are present which is almost diagnostic of an allergic response. Topical antibiotics are not an appropriate treatment choice for patients with seasonal allergic conjunctivitis.

pool.q: When testing visual acuity, what is meant by the crowding phenomenon?

options.a: increase in performance when reading a single optotype compared to a full line
options.b: decrease in performance when Teller acuity cards are held too close to the patient
options.c: decrease in performance after repeated testing
options.d: increase in performance when the patient’s family leaves the examination room

As a result, the measured “linear” acuity of an amblyopic eye can be worse than visual acuity measured with isolated optotypes. For this reason, for the detection of amblyopia, it is best that isolated letters or pictures not be used to test visual acuity.

pool.q: For a pediatric patient diagnosed with Coats disease, what might the ophthalmologist expect to discover in the evaluation?

options.a: subretinal fluid accumulation and intraocular calcification
options.b: a white- to cream-colored mass beneath the retina

pool.rationale:
The classic findings in Coats disease are unilateral yellow subretinal and intraretinal exudates associated with retinal vascular abnormalities--most often telangiectasia, tortuosity, aneurysmal dilatations, and avascularity--with a variable clinical presentation, ranging from mild changes to total retinal detachment (figure). Once the fovea is detached and the subretinal exudate becomes organized, the prognosis for restoration of central vision is poor. Coats disease may mimic retinoblastoma. However, there is no white- to cream-colored mass. Intraocular calcification is extraordinarily rare in Coats disease. The etiology of Coats disease is unknown, but associations with various gene deletions have been reported. Treatment is directed at obliterating the abnormal vessels and includes cryotherapy or laser photocoagulation. The disease is stopped when the leaking vessels are destroyed. Recently, there have been reports of promising results with intravitreal bevacizumab and triamcinolone used as adjuncts to laser treatment.

pool.q: A 12-year-old boy is diagnosed with well-controlled, intermittent exotropia. What is stereopsis testing most likely to reveal?

options.a: no stereopsis because of temporal hemiretinal suppression

In the early stages of the disorder, the deviation is usually larger for distance viewing than for near. Thus, sensory testing at near is typically excellent, including stereopsis and fusion on Worth 4 Dot testing. When the eye deviates, suppression of the image typically occurs, rather than the recognition of diplopia.
