pool.q: What feature is characteristic of congenital ptosis?
pool.rationale: The most common form of congenital ptosis is thought to result from dystrophic development of the levator muscle without associated innervational abnormalities. Patients with congenital ptosis have decreased levator function and a poorly formed eyelid crease. The lid tissues and levator are not longer than normal. Congenital ptosis may be familial and may be unilateral or bilateral. Children with unilateral congenital ptosis will commonly elevate the affected eyelid by lifting the ipsilateral brow. Anisometropic astigmatism may be associated with ptosis and is the most common cause of amblyopia in these patients. Surgical correction serves as definitive treatment for congenital ptosis, and repeat procedures are common. Prompt surgery is recommended for the presence of amblyopia, occlusion of the visual axis, or a severe compensatory head posture (chin-up position).

pool.q: Orbital cellulitis in a 7-year-old patient most commonly arises from where?
pool.rationale: Infectious orbital cellulitis is an infection posterior to the orbital septum. The vast majority of cases are caused by bacterial sinusitis. In a 7-year-old patient, the maxillary and frontal sinuses are underdeveloped. Therefore, orbital cellulitis is most likely to arise from the ethmoidal sinus. Other causative factors include the thinness of the lamina papyracea and venous drainage from the ethmoid sinus to the orbit. In adults, infections are usually polymicrobial, including gram-positive cocci, Moraxella, and H. influenzae. However in children, the causative agent is usually a single organism that is typically a gram-positive organism. Adults often require early surgical intervention, while children typically improve with intravenous antibiotics alone.

pool.q: A 30-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with pseudotumor cerebri, or idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH). Her current medications include lisinopril, tetracycline, vitamin E, and verapamil. What medication should be discontinued?
pool.rationale: Pseudotumor cerebri (or IIH) consists of increased intracranial pressure with normal or small-sized ventricles on neuroimaging and normal cerebrospinal fluid contents. Drugs that have been associated with IIH include tetracycline, corticosteroids, vitamin A, nalidixic acid, thyroid medications, and growth hormones. Medications for the increased intracranial pressure include diuretics, such as acetazolamide and hydrochlorothiazide.

pool.q: A 7-year-old boy is referred for evaluation of a dermolipoma that has been visible in the temporal subconjunctival area since he was an infant. It is becoming larger and cosmetically objectionable, and his parents are requesting its removal. What is the most appropriate course of treatment?

If they become large and cosmetically objectionable, only the anterior, visible portion should be excised. Complete excision of the mass is not appropriate, because it may cause damage to delicate orbital structures. Chemotherapy and radiation would not be expected to have an effect on this slow-growing, benign tumor.

In older children, it is important to obtain their commitment to the treatment program. In compliant patients, improvement is frequent but cannot be guaranteed. pool.q: A 2-year-old with congenital rubella has developed bilateral white cataracts. Five days following uncomplicated right cataract surgery, the child has increased photophobia, redness, and eye pain. What aspect of congenital rubella syndrome most likely explains this development?
pool.rationale:
Live virus particles can be recovered in the eye for up to 3 years after birth in a child with congenital rubella and can cause significant inflammation postsurgically. The vigorous postoperative inflammatory response should be managed aggressively with steroids and mydriatics in these patients because they are prone to secondary membrane development. 
Elevated episcleral venous pressure can result in abnormally high intraocular pressure because episcleral venous pressure accounts for a component of intraocular pressure. Presence of hemoglobin-laden macrophages can cause a secondary glaucoma due to outflow obstruction of the trabecular meshwork in hemolytic glaucoma. Sensitization to native lens proteins refers to phacoantigenic glaucoma in which there is granulomatous inflammation against native lens proteins. None of these are typically associated with congenital rubella syndrome.

pool.q: A newborn is found to have a cloudy central cornea associated with central corneal thinning, adherent lens, and anterior polar cataract. Additionally, the newborn has short stature, cleft lip, and brachydactyly. What is the most likely diagnosis?

If associated with short stature, brachydactyly (short fingers and toes), cleft lip, and intellectual disability, it is Peters-plus syndrome. Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome does not typically have central corneal thinning or adherent lens. Aniridia and Bardet-Biedl syndrome do not have primary corneal abnormalities.

pool.q: What is the most significant risk factor for developing retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)?

pool.q: What topical glaucoma medication is contraindicated in a 2-month-old baby due to risk of central nervous system (CNS) depression associated with bradycardia and apnea?

There may be increased CNS penetration in young children, which can result in CNS depression, bradycardia, apnea, and hypotension in this age group. pool.q: A 14-year-old girl presents for routine eye examination. She has an abduction deficit of the right eye. She is orthophoric in primary gaze. She denies diplopia. What is the most important next step in the examination?

options.a: Observe the lid fissure in attempted right gaze.
options.b: Observe the lid fissure in downgaze.
options.c: Observe the lid fissure in sustained upgaze.
options.d: Observe the lid fissure in left gaze.

pool.rationale:
This girl demonstrates findings of type 1 Duane syndrome, whereby an abduction deficit is present, and the lid fissure narrows on attempted adduction. In anatomical and imaging studies, the nucleus of the sixth cranial nerve is absent, and an aberrant branch of the third cranial nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle. This aberrancy results in firing of both the lateral and medial recti upon attempted adduction, causing globe retraction and narrowing of the interpalpebral fissure. Results of electromyographic studies support this finding. The patient is orthophoric in primary gaze and thus not diplopic, although many patients with type 1 Duane syndrome will have an esotropia at baseline. This condition is considered one entity in a class termed congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders, and it may be associated with systemic defects such as Goldenhar syndrome (hemifacial microsomia, ocular dermoids, ear anomalies, preauricular skin tags, and eyelid colobomas).
Lid position in abduction and downgaze would not be affected in a type 1 Duane syndrome. Lid elevation in downgaze could be seen in aberrant regeneration after a third nerve palsy. Lid position in sustained upgaze would change with myasthenia gravis, causing ptosis with muscle fatigue, but not in Duane syndrome. This patient is not diplopic, indicating a congenital, not acquired etiology such as myasthenia gravis.

pool.q: What is the cause of lid-fissure narrowing on attempted adduction in type 1 Duane syndrome?

options.a: co-contracture of the lateral and medial rectus

pool.rationale: Duane syndrome is an innervational anomaly of the horizontal rectus muscles wherein an aberrant branch of the third cranial nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle. Co-contracture of the medial and lateral rectus muscles on adduction causes globe retraction and secondary lid fissure narrowing (to be clear, it is not that the muscles of the eyelids are contracting and pulling the fissure closed, but rather that the globe's being pulled further back in the orbit is allowing the fissure to get smaller, just as would be true in enophthalmos or an undersized orbital implant after evisceration). Misinnervation of the levator muscle is associated with Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome. Orbicularis oculi spasm is not typically reported in Duane syndrome. Diplopia is rare in Duane syndrome, as suppression develops early in life.

pool.q: An infant is diagnosed with type 1, prethreshold retinopathy of prematurity. What is the best step in management, according to the Early Treatment for Retinopathy of Prematurity (ETROP) study?

options.a: cryotherapy to ablate the peripheral retina
options.d: panretinal laser photocoagulation to ablate the peripheral retina

pool.rationale:
Prethreshold ROP is classified into 2 types. Type 1 includes:
  • zone I, any stage ROP with plus disease
  • zone I, stage 3 ROP, without plus disease
  • zone II, stage 2 or 3 ROP, with plus disease
Type 2 includes:
  • zone 1, stage 1 or 2 ROP, without plus disease
  • zone II, stage 3 ROP, without plus disease.
The ETROP trial found that earlier treatment at prethreshold resulted in better structural and visual outcomes when compared with conventional treatment at threshold. Based on ETROP, laser treatment is recommended for any eye with type 1 ROP. Eyes with type 2 ROP should be closely observed and, if there is progression to type 1 or threshold disease, treated.
Prior to the ETROP trial, the Cryotherapy for Retinopathy of Prematurity (CRYO-ROP) study defined threshold disease as 5 contiguous or 8 total clock hours of stage 3 ROP in zone I or II with plus disease. Laser has largely replaced cryotherapy as treatment for ROP since that time.
The most recent treatment option for type 1 ROP is intravitreal injection of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti­-VEGF) agents bevacizumab and ranibizumab. The initial study of anti­-VEGF agents for treatment of ROP, and the most influential, was Bevacizumab Eliminates the Angiogenic Threat of Retinopathy of Prematurity (BEAT­-ROP), which found a significant benefit to structural outcome for zone I eyes that received intravitreal bevacizumab monotherapy compared with those that received laser treatment. Subsequent publications have docu­mented that ROP may recur months after treatment with anti­-VEGF agents; thus, prolonged surveillance and re­treatment may be necessary after intravitreal anti­-VEGF injections. Anti­-VEGF treatment should not be administered to infants who are unlikely to return for frequent follow-­up examinations after they are discharged from the hospital.

pool.q: To test for a horizontal deviation using the Maddox rod, what direction should the cylinders be oriented in front of the right eye?
pool.rationale: In the Maddox rod test, a series of parallel cylinders convert a single point source of light into a line image perpendicular to the cylinders. To test for horizontal deviations, the Maddox rod cylinders are placed horizontally in front of the right eye (180°). The patient, fixating on a point source of light, sees a vertical line with the right eye and the point source of light with the left. If the line is superimposed on the point, there is no horizontal deviation (orthophoria). If the point is to the left of the line (the line is to the right of the point), esodeviation is present. If the point is to the right of the line (the line is to the left of the point), exodeviation is present.

pool.q: A child has a visual acuity of 20/30 right eye and 20/20 left eye. Cover testing demonstrates a 4 diopter right esotropia. On Worth 4-dot testing, the child sees 3 lights at distance and 4 lights at near. What is this child demonstrating?
pool.rationale:
ARC is a condition wherein the fovea of the fixating eye has acquired an anomalous common visual direction with a peripheral retinal element in the deviating eye. ARC is an adaptation that restores some degree of binocular cooperation despite manifest strabismus. Seeing 4 dots indicates that if there is a suppression scotoma, it must subtend a smaller visual angle than the test target. In this case, the right eye is suppressing the Worth 4-dot at distance, since the lights are being projected into the suppression scotoma. At near, the lights are outside the suppression scotoma and a fused response is noted. This is consistent with ARC.
The child has ARC and monofixation syndrome. The clinician must demonstrate the absence of bimacular fusion by documenting a macular scotoma in the nonfixating eye under binocular conditions, as well as the presence of peripheral binocular vision (peripheral fusion).
A diplopic response or 5 lights would be given at near in normal retinal correspondence in this patient with a right esotropia. If a large suppression scotoma were present, only 3 lights would be seen at near. Paradoxical diplopia occurs when ARC persists following ocular realignment surgery and a previously misaligned eye is now straight.

pool.q: A 3-year-old child is referred to an ophthalmologist for bilateral central corneal opacities and iridocorneal adhesions.  He is noted to have a craniofacial abnormality, intellectual disability, and short stature. What is his most likely condition?
pool.rationale:
Based on this child's presentation, Peters-plus syndrome is the most likely cause. Peters anomaly is characterized by a posterior corneal defect with an overlying stromal opacity, often with adherent iris strands. When unilateral, it is likely isolated, but bilateral cases warrant genetic evaluation. Peters-plus syndrome is caused by biallelic B3GLCT mutations and is associated with short stature, craniofacial abnormalities, shortened fingers and toes, and intellectual disability.
Congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED) does have bilateral corneal haze but is not generally associated with any systemic anomalies. Epibulbar dermoid presents unilaterally in general, and the opacity may vary in size and location on the cornea, limbus, or adjacent sclera; Goldenhar syndrome can be associated with this finding, but its abnormalities include ear deformities, vertebral deformities, eyelid coloboma, or Duane retraction syndrome. Congenital glaucoma can result in bilateral corneal clouding due to high intraocular pressure and may also cause Haab striae and buphthalmos. Primary congenital glaucoma does not have any associated systemic findings.

pool.q: Shortly after scleral buckling surgery and pars plana vitrectomy for retinal detachment repair, a 60-year-old man has pain, conjunctival congestion, a shallow anterior chamber, and marked flare. What is the most likely diagnosis?

pool.q: What category of congenital anomaly is represented by a "typical" iris coloboma?

pool.q: In a child with nystagmus blockage syndrome, what type of strabismic deviation is most commonly present?

pool.q: A healthy 4-year-old boy with normal visual acuity in both eyes has a chin-up posture. What is the most likely cause of this boy's anomalous head position?
pool.rationale:
The most likely cause of this boy's abnormal chin-up position is V-pattern exotropia (figure). A-pattern or V-pattern strabismus occurs in up to one-fourth of all horizontal strabismus cases. Patients with V-pattern forms of strabismus have a horizontal deviation that is more convergent or less divergent in downgaze compared with upgaze. Patients with pattern strabismus and sensory fusion may adopt an anomalous head posture in an effort to maintain a single image, for example, chin-up posture with V-pattern exotropia or chin-down posture with A-pattern exotropia. The etiology of pattern strabismus is unknown except in cases of extraocular muscle palsies. Despite this, multiple theories suggest primary or secondary muscle dysfunction involving the oblique muscles, horizontal rectus muscles, or vertical rectus muscles.
In A-pattern exotropia, a chin-up position would place the eyes in a position of increased exodeviation. Convergence insufficiency and dissociated vertical deviation do not lead to abnormal head positions.

pool.q: A patient presents with orthophoria at distance and 30 prism diopters (30Δ) of esotropia at near. The cycloplegic refraction is -0.25 sphere OU. What is the most common treatment used to decrease the near deviation?

In the setting of an injury, an eccentric or peaked pupil is suggestive of penetrating injury, which requires an examination under anesthesia (EUA) for exploration and repair. Topical antibiotics are not preferred initial treatments. Placing a bandage contact lens or any other device on the eye is contraindicated if there is risk for globe penetration. Associated findings include cognitive disabilities, seizures, facial angiofibromas, ungual or periungual fibromas, ash leaf spots, and shagreen patches. pool.q: A 4-year-old child who has unilateral, chronic uveitis is being treated with cycloplegics. What additional treatment can be done to best prevent amblyopia?
pool.rationale: Cycloplegia is used in uveitis to prevent synechiae formation and decrease pain. However, cycloplegic drugs also blur vision, which can induce amblyopia. Indeed, amblyopia can be treated pharmacologically by using cycloplegics (atropine) on the fellow eye, rather than occlusion therapy, for this reason. Dispensing the full hyperopic prescription with a bifocal gives a clear image at near and distance, to decrease the risk of amblyopia. Orthoptics will not treat amblyopia in this situation. Patching is not the best treatment, as the affected eye will be defocused for near work. Pilocarpine is contraindicated, because it will reverse the beneficial effects of the cycloplegics and may exacerbate inflammation.

pool.q: Correction of what type of refractive error is most likely to lead to an improvement in intermittent exotropia?

pool.q: What finding is an indication for urgent surgical intervention in a pediatric orbital floor fracture?

options.d: involvement of the lacrimal drainage system

pool.rationale:
Upon fracture of the orbital floor, orbital contents may prolapse into the maxillary sinus and become entrapped. Restriction occurs with entrapment of the inferior rectus beneath either a trapdoor fracture or a linear opening caused by flexion deformity of the floor. Injury to the inferior rectus muscle or to its nerve, with resulting weakness, may be caused by hemorrhage or ischemia, in addition to restriction. If muscle entrapment is present, a forced duction test shows restriction of passive movement of the eye. Eye movement may stimulate the oculocardiac reflex, causing pain, nausea, and bradycardia. Urgent repair should be undertaken in these cases, as release of the entrapped muscle may improve the final ocular motility by limiting fibrosis.
Diplopia, orbital ecchymosis, eyelid edema, enophthalmos, hypoesthesia in the cutaneous distribution of the infraorbital nerve, and involvement of the lacrimal drainage system are commonly present with acute orbital fracture but are not indications for urgent repair.

pool.q: The lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) can cause severe congenital infections. By what route or vector is the virus transmitted to the pregnant woman?

pool.q: For a patient with a refraction of +2.00 +3.50 x 90 in the right eye and +1.75 +3.75 x 90 in the left eye, what type of amblyopia is most likely to be present?
pool.rationale:
Meridional amblyopia occurs in the setting of uncorrected high astigmatism, causing loss of resolving ability specific to the chronically blurred meridians. This is a type of isoametropic amblyopia, which is bilateral decreased visual acuity from chronically defocused retinal images. It usually occurs with hyperopia exceeding 4.00 to 5.00 D or myopia exceeding 5.00 to 6.00 D. These types of amblyopia are treated with refractive correction.
Strabismic amblyopia is not typically seen in bilateral astigmatism.
Anisometropic amblyopia occurs in the setting of asymmetric high astigmatism or asymmetric high hyperopia.
Deprivational amblyopia occurs when the visual axis is obstructed, such as in congenital cataracts, severe ptosis, or corneal opacity.

Although some degree of stereopsis can be present in small-angle strabismus with monofixation syndrome, good stereopsis indicates that there is no manifest strabismus and no suppression.

pool.q: How does postoperative steroid treatment in pediatric cataract surgery patients with intraocular lens (IOL) placement compare to such treatment in those without IOL placement?

options.c: Patients with an IOL require the same amount of steroid treatment postoperatively compared to patients without an IOL, as long as the posterior capsule is intact.
options.d: Patients with an IOL require less aggressive steroid treatment postoperatively compared to patients without an IOL.

pool.q: Following several missed follow-up appointments, a 2-year-old child presents for further evaluation of amblyopia in the left eye. Since his last kept appointment, the child has received cycloplegic penalization in the right eye. What problem might the ophthalmologist expect to find?

options.c: worsened vision in the left eye
options.d: increased myopia in the right eye

pool.rationale: Patient and parent counseling regarding treatment and side effects are a fundamental part of amblyopia management because patient and parent compliance and cooperation are crucial to a successful functional or visual outcome. As a result, the better eye experiences blur with near viewing and, with uncorrected hyperopia, with distance viewing as well. Regular follow-up of amblyopic patients on treatment with cycloplegia is necessary to avoid reverse amblyopia to the contralateral eye. Pharmacologic penalization has been used to successfully treat moderate levels of amblyopia. The child described is not likely to have experienced decreased vision in the originally amblyopic (left) eye. Increased myopia in the right eye or increased hyperopia in the left eye are not risks associated with the use of pharmacologic penalization.

pool.q: A patient is diagnosed with inferior oblique muscle overaction. What would the most likely findings be on versions testing?

options.b: overelevation of the affected eye in adduction
options.c: overelevation of the affected eye in primary position
options.d: overelevation of the affected eye in abduction

pool.rationale: The actions of the inferior oblique vary in different gazes because the muscle axis is not parallel with the visual axis. In abduction, the primary action is extorsion. Therefore, an overacting inferior oblique will show overelevation in adduction primarily.

Whether the surgery is done on an outpatient or inpatient basis, the patient must be examined on the day after the surgery. pool.q: What is the most likely mechanism of glaucoma in Sturge-Weber syndrome?

pool.q: What is the earliest sign of malignant hyperthermia?

options.a: unexplained elevation of end-tidal carbon dioxide concentration

pool.rationale:
Malignant hyperthermia is a sporadic or autosomal dominantly inherited disorder characterized by a defect of calcium binding by the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscle. Intracellular calcium levels can rise dramatically causing muscle contraction with acidosis, heat production, hyperkalemia, and muscle breakdown. Clinically the patient may have muscle rigidity, tachypnea, tachycardia, sweating, cyanosis, skin discoloration, or dark urine. The disorder is triggered by certain inhalational anesthetics or succinylcholine, and the earliest sign is unexplained elevation of end-tidal carbon dioxide concentration. If untreated, malignant hyperthermia can be fatal. Treatment involves dantrolene and should be managed by the anesthesia team.

Both peribulbar and retrobulbar anesthesia make most EOM procedures pain-­free and should be considered in adults for whom general anesthesia may pose an undue hazard. The administration of a short-­acting hypnotic by an anesthesiologist just before retrobulbar injection greatly improves patient comfort. ­Because injected anesthetics may influence alignment during the first few hours ­after surgery, suture adjustment is best delayed for at least half a day.
General anesthesia is necessary for ­children and is often used for adults as well, particularly ­those requiring bilateral surgery. Neuromuscular blocking agents such as succinylcholine, which are administered to facilitate intubation for general anesthesia, can temporarily affect the results of a traction test. Nondepolarizing agents, which do not have this effect, can be used instead.
Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting
Eye muscle surgery is a risk ­factor for postoperative nausea and vomiting. This risk can be reduced by prophylaxis with dexamethasone and serotonin type 3 (5-­HT3) antagonists (eg, ondansetron), propofol use, adequate hydration, and reduced use of inhalation anesthetics and opioid analgesia.
Oculocardiac Reflex
The oculocardiac reflex is a slowing of the heart rate caused by traction on the EOMs, particularly the medial rectus muscle. In its most severe form, the reflex can produce asystole. The surgeon should be aware of the possibility of inducing the oculocardiac reflex when manipulating a muscle and should be prepared to release tension if the heart rate drops excessively. Intravenous atropine and other agents can protect against this reflex.
Malignant Hyperthermia
Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is an impor­tant disorder for pediatric ophthalmologists ­because of its association with strabismus, myopathies, ptosis, and musculoskeletal abnormalities. MH is a defect of calcium binding by the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscle that can occur sporadically or be dominantly inherited with incomplete penetrance. When MH is triggered by inhalational anesthetics or the muscle relaxant succinylcholine, unbound intracellular calcium concentration increases. This stimulates muscle contracture, causing massive acidosis. In its fully developed form, MH is characterized by extreme heat production, resulting from the hypermetabolic state.
MH can be fatal if diagnosis and treatment are delayed. The earliest sign is unexplained elevation of end-­tidal carbon dioxide concentration. As soon as the diagnosis is made, surgery should be terminated, even if incomplete.

pool.q: A 4-month-old boy does not fix or follow but has an otherwise normal eye examination. The child is re-examined when he is 6 months old and is noted to have normal responses to visual stimuli. What is the most likely diagnosis?

The term delayed visual maturation (DVM) describes a condition wherein normal fixation and tracking do not develop within the first 3-4 months of life, but visual behavior subsequently normalizes.
Cerebral visual impairment (CVI) is caused by pathology posterior to the lateral geniculate nucleus. CVI can be congenital or acquired. Causes include structural central nervous system (CNS) abnormalities, intrauterine infection, periventricular leukomalacia, hypoxia, hydrocephalus, abusive head trauma, and encephalitis. pool.q: What feature characterizes central fusion disruption?

Patients with central fusion disruption have misalignment of the visual axes and intractable diplopia. The angle of strabismus can be small or may vary. The patients do not have any fusion or fusional amplitudes. The patients have double vision because they lack sensory adaptations of suppression, or anomalous retinal correspondence.

pool.q: What method is recommended for assessing the refractive state in amblyopia?
pool.rationale:
Cycloplegic retinoscopy is the most objective and accurate method to determine the ocular refractive state in amblyopia. Due to the large accommodative capacity and tone in children, cycloplegia is necessary to accurately determine the full refractive error, especially in patients with hyperopia. Therapy for refractive amblyopia is predicated upon correcting the full refractive error of the amblyopic eye(s) and penalizing the least amblyopic or non-amblyopic eye. Because an amblyopic eye’s ability to control accommodation tends to be impaired, this eye cannot be relied on to compensate for uncorrected hyperopia as would a normal child’s eye.
Retinoscopy under anesthesia (but without complete cycloplegia), manifest refraction, and autorefraction are not satisfactory, because they may not determine the full optical refractive state in the highly accommodative pediatric eye.

pool.q: What is the most frequent cause of childhood visual impairment in developed countries?
pool.rationale:
Visual dysfunction in infants and children is classified into 3 major categories:
  • delayed visual maturation
  • pregeniculate visual impairment
  • retrogeniculate visual impairment
Cognitive impairment, though it can affect the language-learning ability and other visually oriented skills, is not a classification of visual dysfunction.
Delayed visual maturation occurs when normal visual fixation and tracking does not develop within the first 3 months of life. Pregeniculate visual impairment refers to visual deficits related to pathology anterior to the lateral geniculate nucleus. Retrogeniculate visual impairment (also termed cerebral visual impairment [CVI]) refers to visual deficits related to pathology posterior to the lateral geniculate nucleus. Retrogeniculate visual impairment is the most frequent cause of childhood visual impairment in developed countries.
Amblyopic visual deficits result primarily from visual cortical changes. With abnormal visual experience early in life, cells of the primary visual cortex can lose their ability to respond to stimulation of 1 or both eyes, and the cells that remain responsive show significant functional deficiencies, including abnormally large receptive fields. For this reason, amblyopia would be considered a retrogeniculate cause of vision loss.

pool.q: A toddler with esotropia since infancy and severe amblyopia in the left eye develops a prominent, conjugate, horizontal jerk nystagmus that is right-beating in both right gaze and left gaze. What is this the most likely cause of this condition?

options.a: acquired vestibular nystagmus superimposed on infantile esotropia syndrome
options.b: infantile nystagmus syndrome with secondary nystagmus blockage syndrome
options.c: infantile nystagmus syndrome with null point in extreme left gaze
options.d: manifest latent nystagmus with infantile esotropia syndrome

pool.rationale:
Latent nystagmus is a marker of fusional maldevelopment. Latent nystagmus can become manifest when only 1 eye is being used for vision, such as in amblyopia.
A null point in left gaze would be expected to dampen nystagmus in left gaze. Vestibular nystagmus is periodic alternating nystagmus, an unusual form of congenital motor jerk nystagmus that periodically changes directions. Infantile nystagmus syndrome would become manifest in infancy.

pool.q: Pseudoesotropia can be associated with what other finding?
pool.rationale: Pseudoesotropia occurs when facial features cause tissue to obscure the nasal sclera, leading to the appearance that the eyes are directed inward. Pseudoesotropia is usually associated with a reduced interpupillary distance or prominent epicanthal folds. No real deviation exists, and the results of both corneal light reflex testing and cover-uncover testing are normal. As the child grows, the pseudoesotropia is usually reduced or resolves. Temporal retinal dragging may cause pseudoexotropia.

pool.q: A patient undergoes a retrobulbar anesthetic injection just prior to glaucoma filtering surgery. What change in eye position is the surgeon likely to observe intraoperatively?

options.b: incyclotorsion and depression of the eye
options.d: excyclotorsion and elevation of the eye

pool.rationale:
A retrobulbar injection introduces anesthetic into the intraconal space, an extension of the fascial planes of the annulus of Zinn. The annulus of Zinn is formed by the 4 rectus muscle insertions and their intermuscular fascia; it encompasses the optic canal and splits the superior orbital fissure into an intraconal and extraconal compartment (Figure 1). The intraconal compartment contains both divisions of the oculomotor (III) and abducens (VI) nerves. Also recall that the nerve to the inferior oblique muscle travels in the inferior branch of the oculomotor nerve. Therefore, abduction, supraduction, and excyclotorsion would not occur, as these motor nerves have been anesthetized by the retrobulbar block. The trochlear nerve (IV) lies outside the annulus of Zinn in the extraconal space, and is often spared during retrobulbar blocks, resulting in intact incyclotorsion and infraduction of the globe intraoperatively.
Figure 1. The four rectus muscles and their intermuscular fascial attachments form the annulus of Zinn. A: Optic canal. B: Superior division of the oculomotor nerve (III). C: The nasociliary nerve (V-1), supplying sensory innervation to the globe. D: The inferior division of III. E: The lacrimal nerve (V-1). F: The frontal nerve (V-1). G: The trochlear nerve (IV). H: The abducens nerve (VI). Note that the superior orbital vein (blue) is variably drawn as intraconal or extraconal, depending on the atlas.

pool.q: What intracranial structural abnormality could account for new-onset downbeat nystagmus in a 4-year-old girl?
pool.rationale: Less than 20% of childhood nystagmus is acquired and necessitates further imaging. Downbeat nystagmus is usually acquired secondary to Arnold-Chiari malformation. Pinealoma is associated with convergence-retraction nystagmus. Chiasmal tumors have been associated with spasmus nutans, a triad of nystagmus, head bobbing, and torticollis. Craniopharyngioma is associated with see-saw nystagmus.

pool.q: For patients with Duane syndrome, what is the preferred surgical procedure to treat upshoots and downshoots?

options.a: recession of the medial rectus muscle
options.b: Y-splitting of the medial rectus muscle
options.c: resection of the lateral rectus muscle
options.d: Y-splitting of the lateral rectus muscle

pool.rationale:
Y-splitting of the lateral rectus muscle is the preferred surgical therapeutic option for upshoots and downshoots in patients with Duane syndrome. Additional options to address the upshoots and downshoots include large lateral rectus recession, retroequatorial fixation of the lateral rectus muscle, and more recently, deactivation of the lateral rectus muscle and reattachment to the lateral periosteum of the orbit with a subsequent transposition procedure.
Surgical therapy for strabismus from Duane syndrome depends upon the deviation pattern and includes transposition of the vertical rectus muscles and recession of the medial rectus muscle on the affected side with or without recession of the medial rectus muscle on the opposite side. Transposition procedures and recession of the medial rectus muscles, however, do not address upshoots and downshoots. Surgical intervention should not be performed in patients who have binocular vision with the eyes in primary position or for binocularity achieved with an acceptably slight head turn.

pool.q: What extraocular muscle is responsible for elevation of the eye in adduction?
pool.rationale: The movements of the vertical and oblique muscles are complex because in primary position, the muscle axes are not in alignment with the visual axis. Therefore, when an eye is adducted, the inferior oblique is the primary elevator. The superior rectus is the primary elevator in abduction. Neither the superior oblique nor inferior rectus muscles are elevators of the eye.

pool.q: A 23-year-old man was recently found to have convergence paralysis. In addition to diplopia at near, the patient notes blurred vision when focusing on near objects. What can be done to minimize the patient's symptoms?

options.a: a trial of plus lenses with base-in prisms for near work
options.b: a trial of plus lenses, followed by bilateral medial rectus muscle resection
options.c: a trial of base-in prisms for near work
options.d: a trial of base-in prisms, followed by bilateral medial rectus muscle resection

pool.rationale: Convergence paralysis results in an exotropia at near. Base-in prisms will help move the images toward the apex of the prism to alleviate the diplopia. Blurred vision at near suggests an accompanying accommodative insufficiency component that can occur with convergence paralysis. Thus, plus lenses at near would be required in addition to the base-in prism. Surgery is not a good option, since this will alter the alignment in the distance. Usually, convergence paralysis occurs secondary to an intracranial lesion.

pool.q: A child presents for evaluation of allergic conjunctivitis. She continues to experience puffy, red, watery, itchy eyes despite using an oral antihistamine. What is the preferred management?
pool.rationale: After confirming the findings that support the diagnosis of allergic conjunctivitis, the ophthalmologist needs to modify this patient's treatment plan, because it is not effective. Seasonal allergic conjunctivitis tends to occur in the spring and fall and is triggered by environmental contact with specific airborne allergens such as pollens from grasses, flowers, weeds, and trees. Patients typically present with reddened, watery eyes, boggy-appearing conjunctiva, and complaints of itchy eyes. If scrapings of the conjunctiva are obtained in patients with allergic conjunctivitis, eosinophils are present. Management of allergic conjunctivitis involves removal of the offending allergens from the patient's environment and initiating systemic and/or topical medications. Cool compresses to the eyes can further increase patient comfort. In this case, the patient was started on oral antihistamines. Oral antihistamines tend to be less effective at relieving specific ocular symptoms but are especially useful in cases where other symptoms, such as nasal congestion, are present. In this case, an H1-receptor blocker or mast cell stabilizing drop is preferred. Mast cell stabilizing drugs are not offered as options here. Mild topical corticosteroid drops should be reserved for severe or recalcitrant cases. Patients, especially children, treated with topical corticosteroids need to be monitored closely for steroid adverse effects, such as cataracts or glaucoma.

pool.q: A toddler presents with ptosis and a chin-up position. What is the most important determinant in choosing the surgical technique for repair?
pool.rationale:
The levator function is the most important determinant of the type of surgical repair to employ. Moderate to good levator function can often benefit from a levator resection. Poor levator function requires a frontalis sling approach to recruit the brow musculature to lift the lid.
The age of the patient, the presence of amblyopia, and the presence of associated syndromes can be important determinants for the timing of surgical repair.

pool.q: A 6-year-old boy with neuroblastoma is found to have acquired Horner syndrome. What is the most likely site of the causative neuroblastoma?
pool.rationale: Horner syndrome can occur from a primary cervical or apical thoracic neuroblastoma that involves the sympathetic chain. While neuroblastoma is the most common cause of metastatic orbital malignancy in children, Horner syndrome does not occur from metastatic neuroblastoma. Neuroblastoma usually arises from the adrenal gland or sympathetic ganglion chain in the mediastinum or retroperitoneum.

pool.q: An infant is noted to have leukocoria, microphthalmos, and elongated ciliary processes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: All of the listed conditions (ROP, Coats disease, retinoblastoma) can present with leukocoria, but only persistent fetal vasculature is associated with microphthalmia. PFV results from failed regression of the fetal hyaloid vasculature. Findings can vary from a retrolental membrane to a stalk connecting the lens and optic nerve. It is also associated with elongated ciliary processes, cataract and retinal detachment, and angle closure glaucoma.

pool.q: A patient presents with transient episodes of convergence, accommodative spasm, and miosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Spasm of the near reflex is a condition with excessive convergence, excessive accommodation, and miosis. Patients often present with episodes of esotropia alternating with orthophoria. The etiology generally is thought to be functional, although it rarely can be associated with organic disease. Treatment consists of cycloplegic agents such as atropine and homatropine, hyperopic correction, bifocal glasses, and/or counseling to address underlying psychologic issues.
Cyclic esotropia has periods of esotropia and orthophoria, but it is not associated with miosis or accommodative spasm. Divergence insufficiency has esotropia worse at distance than near, and no pupillary abnormalities. Convergence insufficiency shows decreased convergence, not excess convergence.

pool.q: In a patient with epidemic keratoconjunctivitis, what is the most appropriate indication for treatment with topical corticosteroids?
pool.rationale:
Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis is a highly contagious viral conjunctivitis that is usually self-limited. Treatment is usually supportive, with cold compresses and artificial tears. The complication of subepithelial corneal opacities is sometimes treated with topical steroids. 
Epiphora and periorbital pain are common symptoms that do not require steroid treatment. Periorbital ecchymosis does not require steroid treatment but may be a sign of preseptal cellulitis.

pool.q: What is the most appropriate surgery to perform for a V-pattern esotropia with no inferior oblique overaction?

options.a: bilateral medial rectus recession with superior transposition (superoplacement)
options.b: unilateral medial rectus recession and lateral rectus resection with inferior transposition (inferoplacement)
options.c: bilateral medial rectus recession with inferior transposition (inferoplacement)
options.d: bilateral lateral rectus resection with inferior transposition (inferoplacement)

pool.rationale: In a V-pattern esotropia, the medial rectus muscles can be recessed and moved toward the apex of the deviation, which would be inferiorly in this case. Lateral muscles should be moved away from the apex of the deviation. A useful mnemonic is MALE: medial rectus muscle to the apex, lateral rectus muscle to the empty space. When horizontal muscle recession-resection is performed, displacement should be in opposite directions, but this will cause symptomatic torsion if the patient has vision in the eye.

pool.q: For a child with optic nerve hypoplasia, what visual acuity would be consistent with the diagnosis?

options.a: 20/400 to light perception correlating well with disc size
options.b: 20/400 to light perception correlating well to the integrity of the macular fibers
options.c: 20/20 to no light perception correlating well with disc size
options.d: 20/20 to no light perception correlating well to the integrity of the macular fibers

pool.rationale:
Optic nerve hypoplasia (ONH) is characterized by small optic discs on fundus examination. Although a decreased number of optic nerve axons may be present histologically, this cannot be quantified premortem. Visual acuity can range from normal (20/20) to no light perception and is related to the integrity of the macular fibers, rather than disc size. Clinically, the disc is pale or gray and smaller than normal. This condition can be unilateral or bilateral and is often asymmetric, as shown. It may be associated with a yellow to white ring around the disc (double ring sign). Visual acuity in patients with optic nerve hypoplasia often does not correlate with the overall size of the disc or the amount of visual field constriction. Frequently, visual fields contain localized defects combined with visual field constriction but these do not correlate to disc size. Patients with ONH may have any combination of absence of the septum pellucidum, agenesis of the corpus callosum, cerebral hemisphere abnormalities, and pituitary gland abnormalities.

pool.q: What type of exodeviation are orthoptic exercises the most appropriate initial therapy for?
pool.rationale: Orthoptic training to stimulate convergence might improve the deviation in patients with convergence insufficiency, a type of convergence weakness exotropia. Patients with Duane retraction syndrome might present with exotropia due to decreased adduction. Dissociated strabismus might manifest with an exodeviation. Both Duane retraction syndrome and dissociated strabismus are treated surgically. Positive angle kappa is a form of pseudostrabismus, in which the eyes appear exotropic, but the visual axes are optically aligned.

pool.q: A 5-year-old boy has a history of bilateral superior oblique palsy. Cover testing would be expected to reveal what deviation and pattern?
pool.rationale:
Bilateral superior oblique palsy occurs commonly after head trauma but is sometimes congenital. Unlike the unilateral superior oblique palsies, it is associated with a V-pattern esotropia and excyclotorsion greater than 10°.
V-pattern esotropia with incyclotorsion is seen in skew deviations, an important differential to exclude in cases of closed head injury. A-pattern strabismus is not typically seen in association with superior oblique palsy. It occurs most commonly in patients with exotropia and persons with spina bifida.

pool.q: A 68-year-old woman has a large esodeviation secondary to a complete sixth nerve palsy OD that has not resolved for 9 months. She cannot abduct past midline. What treatment would you recommend?

options.a: botulinum toxin injection to the ipsilateral medial rectus muscle
options.c: large resection of the involved lateral rectus muscle with recession of the ipsilateral medial rectus muscle

pool.rationale: Surgery for the treatment of 6th nerve palsy is indicated when spontaneous resolution does not occur after 6 months or more of follow-up. In patients with some lateral rectus muscle function, a large recession of the antagonist medial rectus muscle, combined with resection of the lateral rectus muscle, is appropriate. However, in cases of total paralysis like this one, a vertical muscle transposition procedure is usually required. Botulinum toxin injection into the ipsilateral medial rectus muscle can be used initially to balance the paretic lateral rectus muscle while waiting for potential spontaneous improvement in 6th nerve function. Orthoptic exercises would not be useful.

pool.q: A child is uncooperative during the eye examination. What is the most appropriate step to take?

options.a: Schedule the patient for an immediate examination under anesthesia.
options.c: Try a combination of rest periods, persistence, and, if necessary, a return visit.

pool.rationale: Most infants and children can be examined successfully in the office. A combination of persuasion, rest, playing, and in some cases rescheduling for a different day may be necessary. The practitioner needs to balance the emotional consequences of restraint for the patient and caregivers. An examination under anesthesia may become necessary if an adequate examination cannot be performed in the office.

pool.q: A 13-day-old infant presents with esotropia and poor suck reflex from bilateral facial weakness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Möbius syndrome is a congenital dysinnervation syndrome presenting as combined cranial nerve VI and VII paresis, as well as limb, chest, and tongue defects. This syndrome produces facial weakness and esotropia with horizontal gaze palsies, due to aplasia of the CN VI nucleus and involvement of other pontine structures.
The main differential diagnosis is congenital myasthenia gravis. A transient neonatal form, caused by the placental transfer of acetylcholine receptor antibodies of mothers with myasthenia gravis, usually subsides rapidly. Ptosis is present in over 90% of these patients and would be seen more commonly than facial weakness.
Botulinum toxin could also be a cause of facial weakness and ophthalmoplegia, but is likely to produce bilateral ptosis and poor pupillary reactivity in addition.
Duane syndrome is another congenital innervational ophthalmoplegia syndrome; it affects CN III and CN VI, often causing esotropia with lid fissure narrowing on attempted adduction due to co-contraction of the medial and lateral recti. Duane syndrome is not associated with facial paresis.

pool.q: What is the most common ophthalmologic manifestation of abusive head trauma?
pool.rationale: Retinal hemorrhages are the cardinal manifestation of abusive head trauma (AHT, formerly termed shaken baby syndrome). The incidence of retinal hemorrhages in AHT is approximately 80%. Classically, children with AHT have retinal hemorrhages that are multilayered: preretinal, intraretinal, and subretinal. Papilledema occurs in less than 10% of cases of AHT. Cranial nerve paresis and exudative retinal detachment are not commonly associated with AHT.

pool.q: What is the primary purpose of the 4-diopter base-out prism test?

options.a: It is the most reliable method of documenting a macular suppression scotoma.
options.b: It is used to show that patients with bifixation will have a convergence response.
options.c: It is used to document a facultative scotoma in a patient with no manifest deviation.
options.d: It demonstrates that when the prism is placed over the nonfixating eye, the contralateral eye will converge.

pool.rationale:
The 4-diopter base out prism test is used to document the presence of a small macular scotoma in a patient with monofixation syndrome and either a microstrabismus or no manifest deviation. When the prism is placed over the nonfixating eye, there is no movement of the eye and no convergence movement of the contralateral eye.
This is the least reliable test to document a macular suppression scotoma because patients with monofixation syndrome might switch fixation and patients with bifixation might recognize the diplopic response, but make no convergence movements. While a normal patient (a patient with bifixation) would demonstrate the convergence behavior, it is not the purpose of the test to demonstrate this.

pool.q: A 5-year-old boy is found to have decreased vision in his left eye. The visual acuity is 20/25 in his right eye and 20/60 in his left eye. Cycloplegic retinoscopy is +1.00 sphere in the right eye and +1.75 sphere in the left eye. The sensorimotor examination is consistent with 25 prism diopters of esotropia. What is the most likely cause of the patient's decreased vision?
pool.rationale: Amblyopia is a unilateral or, less commonly, bilateral reduction of best-corrected visual acuity that cannot be attributed directly to the effect of any structural abnormality of the eye or posterior visual pathways. Etiologies include strabismic, anisometropic, isoametropic (high bilateral refractive error), or deprivation. In this case, the patient has an esotropia; thus, strabismus is the cause.

pool.q: Patients found to have gonococcal conjunctivitis should also be treated for what common coinfection?
pool.rationale: Up to one-third of patients with gonococcal conjunctivitis have been reported to have concurrent chlamydial venereal disease. Because of this frequent association, it is advisable to give patients supplemental oral antibiotics for treatment of chlamydial infection. The other 3 infectious agents (hepatitis C virus, herpes simplex virus, and syphilis) are not found with high coinfection frequency.

pool.q: What are the typical ocular findings in patients with the tubulointerstitial nephritis uveitis (TINU) syndrome?
pool.rationale: In addition to systemic manifestations necessary for this diagnosis (elevated blood creatinine levels, proteinuria, β2-microglobulinuria, normoglycemic glycosuria, abnormal liver function test results [LFTs], eosinophilia, fevers, arthralgias, myalgias, rash), patients with TINU present with an acute, often bilateral, nongranulomatous anterior uveitis. While the eyes can also become injected as a result of the iritis, this is not a scleritis. Posterior segment manifestations are atypical of this syndrome.

pool.q: In patients with aniridia, what is the most common cause of progressive corneal scarring?
pool.rationale:
Aniridia is due to a mutation of the PAX6 gene and is inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion. Sporadic cases also occur and are associated with Wilms tumor. Patients with congenital aniridia can develop progressive corneal scarring within the first decade of life, necessitating corneal transplantation to restore vision. Adult patients with aniridia can also develop later-onset issues with non-healing epithelial defects and corneal neovascularization. The major underlying mechanism is related to limbal stem cell deficiency, although abnormal cell differentiation may play a role as well.
Herpes simplex keratitis can be a cause of progressive corneal scarring, but it is more common in atopic patients, not aniridic patients. Endothelial decompensation can be seen in Peters anomaly patients, but is not typical of aniridia. Patients with aniridia are more prone to have ptosis than exposure keratopathy.
